# effect-spacetimedb

> Effect-native builders and client wrappers for typed SpaceTimeDB modules.

This file indexes the documentation site at https://effect-stdb.dev. Each docs page is listed with a URL and summary so agents can choose the right source quickly. Raw markdown is also emitted at matching `.md` paths.

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/codegen

---
draft: false
title: Codegen
description: Use native generation directly, or quarantine generated source behind a spec-typed facade.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/codegen" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Codegen ↗</a>

SpacetimeDB remains the source of truth for native client generation. Build the
module, then run `spacetime generate` against the built bundle:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "spacetime build --module-path .",
    "generate-client": "spacetime generate --lang typescript --js-path ./dist/bundle.js --out-dir ./src/generated --yes"
  }
}
```

The `spacetime` CLI has to match the `spacetimedb` package the module depends
on. `spacetime build` and `spacetime generate` read and write a
version-specific module-definition format, so a mismatched CLI either refuses
the module or emits bindings a host of the other version rejects. Move the CLI,
the package, and the server together.

This is the default path. In an ordinary strict TypeScript project, import the
generated `DbConnection` and pass it directly to the Effect client:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule
declare const DbConnection: StdbClient.GeneratedWsConnectionFactory<
  typeof Module.spec,
  unknown
>
declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const WsLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
})
```

## Quarantined bindings for stricter projects

Some projects enable additional compiler settings that make third-party
generated source undesirable in their type graph. The published
`effect-spacetimedb/codegen` API preserves upstream runtime behavior while
quarantining that source. It accepts a prebuilt module bundle, runs the native
generator into staging, and emits only `index.js` plus a small erased
`index.d.ts`.

```ts
import * as NodeServices from "@effect/platform-node/NodeServices"
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import {
  checkArtifact,
  generateArtifact,
} from "effect-spacetimedb/codegen"

const target = {
  moduleBundlePath: "dist/bundle.js",
  stagingDir: ".tmp/effect-spacetimedb-codegen/staging",
  artifactDir: "src/generated-client",
  spacetimeCommand: ["spacetime"],
}

const program = process.argv.includes("--check")
  ? checkArtifact(target)
  : generateArtifact(target)

await Effect.runPromise(program.pipe(Effect.provide(NodeServices.layer)))
```

Run this script without `--check` to emit the artifact. Use `--check` in CI to
regenerate in staging and compare without rewriting the committed artifact.
Add `.tmp/` to the consumer project's `.gitignore` so generated staging files
cannot be committed accidentally.

The codegen export runs under plain Node 20 or newer. Install `esbuild@^0.25` as
an optional peer and provide the platform layer at your executable boundary;
the example uses `@effect/platform-node`'s `NodeServices.layer`. The pipeline
asserts the exact SpaceTimeDB CLI version it was built against before
generating, and fails with `CodegenCliVersionError` on anything else.

The artifact declaration is deliberately erased. Restore type identity in one
hand-written facade tied to the same module contract used by the server:

```ts
import {
  generatedConnection,
  type GeneratedConnectionOf,
} from "effect-spacetimedb/client"
import { DbConnection as GeneratedDbConnection } from "./generated-client/index.js"
import { Module } from "./module"

export const DbConnection: GeneratedConnectionOf<typeof Module.spec> =
  generatedConnection(Module.spec, GeneratedDbConnection)
```

Import the facade everywhere else. `generatedConnection(...)` is an identity at
runtime; the generated JavaScript still comes entirely from
`spacetime generate`, so upstream retains SDK and wire compatibility. Generated
sessions also validate that every public table, public event table, and public
view in the contract exists on the built connection and fail with
`GeneratedArtifactShapeError`, naming the missing keys, when the artifact is
stale.

## Accessor Keys Are camelCase

`spacetime generate` keys the generated `db` and `tables` accessors by the
**camelCase** spelling of each relation's name, and emits a `@deprecated`
snake_case alias wherever the two spellings differ.

effect-spacetimedb resolves tables, event tables, and views alike by their
**contract key** — the key you wrote in `addTables(...)` or the views group.
Declared names are required to be camelCase-canonical, so the contract key is
the generated accessor key under either name policy, and the deprecated aliases
are never resolved. A client that exposes only the alias is treated as stale and
fails acquisition with `GeneratedArtifactShapeError`.

Only SQL and subscription text keeps the wire name. A module on the
`snake_case` policy still queries `all_users` while its rows arrive through the
`allUsers` accessor.

## Never Format A Generated Artifact

Both the artifact pipeline's `--check` mode and drift checks compare generated
files by content. A formatter run over `src/generated` or `src/generated-client`
rewrites bytes the generator did not produce and turns every subsequent check
red, with a diff that looks like real drift. Exclude the directory *and its
contents* from your formatter — a directory-only pattern does not stop a
pre-commit hook that passes explicit file paths:

```json
{
  "files": {
    "includes": ["**", "!src/generated-client", "!src/generated-client/**"]
  }
}
```

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/connection

---
draft: false
title: Client Connection
description: Project a module contract into typed HTTP and WebSocket clients.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/connection" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Client Connection ↗</a>

`Stdb.project(Module)` produces a client-safe projection. It contains no
server runtime; it is only the callable, route, table, and subscription shape
needed by clients.

## HTTP Client

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule
declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const HttpLive = Example.client.http.layer({ uri, databaseName, token })

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  yield* client.reducers.user_upsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
}).pipe(Effect.provide(HttpLive))
```

Typed HTTP handlers are called with just their payload. Raw handlers take the
payload and request options.

## Effect HttpApi Projection

Typed `post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can be projected into a stock Effect
`HttpApi`:

```ts
const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)
```

This is useful when callers already use `HttpApiClient.make(...)` and want
status-based declared-error decoding.

## WebSocket Client

WebSocket sessions use generated native bindings through
`effect-spacetimedb/client`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule
declare const DbConnection: StdbClient.GeneratedWsConnectionFactory<
  typeof Module.spec,
  unknown
>
declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const WsLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated({
  DbConnection,
  uri,
  databaseName,
  token,
})
```

`layerGenerated` and `scopedGenerated` are the generated-client paths. The
standalone generated config helper is reserved for the package testing
entrypoint.

Named tags let one process hold multiple sessions for the same module.

```typescript twoslash
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule
declare const DbConnection: StdbClient.GeneratedWsConnectionFactory<
  typeof Module.spec,
  unknown
>
declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const MainSession = Example.client.ws.tag("main")
const MainLive = Example.client.ws.layerGenerated(
  { DbConnection, uri, databaseName, token },
  { name: "main" },
)
```

The native generated client still owns the actual WebSocket
connection. effect-spacetimedb layers typed Effect services, scoped sessions,
and projected HTTP clients over the module contract.

## Connection Failures

The handshake is the dividing line. A failure before the connection is
established fails the scoped acquisition with `WsConnectError`; a failure after
it is a connection loss, which invalidates the session and fails in-flight and
subsequent calls with `ConnectionLostError`.

| What happened | During acquisition | On an established session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Socket error before the handshake | `WsConnectError` with the socket error as `cause` | — |
| Socket error after the handshake | `WsConnectError` with the socket error as `cause` | `ConnectionLostError` whose `raw` is that error's message |
| Close with no reported error | `WsConnectError` with `cause: undefined` | `ConnectionLostError` with `raw: "WebSocket connection disconnected"` |
| Connect timeout | `WsConnectError` whose `cause` is `WsConnectTimeoutError` | — |
| Generated client missing contract relations | `GeneratedArtifactShapeError`, naming the missing keys | — |

A socket error raised *after* the handshake never arrives as a connect error.
The SDK records it, closes the socket, and reports it on the disconnect path, so
`cause` is what distinguishes a connection that died with a reason from one that
simply closed. The causeless case covers both a clean close and the close the
SDK performs when an inbound frame fails to decompress.

In a browser, `onerror` hands the SDK an `ErrorEvent` rather than an `Error`.
The SDK normalizes that to an `Error` carrying the event's message, with the
original event on `.cause`, so `WsConnectError.cause` is an `Error` on every
runtime.

`ConnectionLostError` means the client never observed a terminal response for a
call. The reducer or procedure may already have committed on the server. Treat
the outcome as unknown, prefer idempotent mutations, and reconcile from the
replacement session's subscribed state before retrying anything that is not.

A bare scoped session surfaces terminal invalidation and stops there. Long-lived
clients can opt into the package supervisor for bounded acquisition, jittered
reconnect backoff, scoped per-session setup, and resubscription; a reconnect
after a causeless close behaves exactly like one after a reported socket error.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/clients/sdk-api

---
draft: false
title: SDK API
description: Use the projected Effect HTTP client, WebSocket session, targets, and HttpApi projection.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/api" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: SDK API ↗</a>

`Stdb.project(Module)` is the Effect-native SDK companion for a module.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_upsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const HttpLive = Example.client.http.layer({ uri, databaseName, token })

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  yield* client.Users.reducers.user_upsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
}).pipe(Effect.provide(HttpLive))
```

The projection contains:

- `client.http`: typed Effect service, direct `make`, and layer constructors.
- `client.ws`: scoped/layered WebSocket sessions over generated native bindings.
- `targets`: public persistent-table, event-table, and all-public-table targets.
- `module`, `tables`, `reducers`, `procedures`, `httpHandlers`, and `lifecycle`
  metadata for tooling.
- `Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)`: an Effect `HttpApi` projection for typed HTTP
  routes.

effect-spacetimedb's client surface uses Effect services and
typed errors. It does not replace the native generated WebSocket cache; it wraps
it with scoped resources, projected callables, and subscription helpers.

Every key in the projection — table, event-table, and view keys passed to
`subscribe`, `streamTable`, `targets`, and the session's `db` — is the
**contract key** you declared, which is also the camelCase accessor key
`spacetime generate` emits. The wire name appears only inside SQL and
subscription text. See [Codegen](/core-concepts/clients/codegen).

## Group-Scoped HTTP Clients

The HTTP client keeps its flat `reducers`, `procedures`, and `httpHandlers`
records and also projects every authored group as a namespace:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_upsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
  Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("user_get", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() })),
  }),
)
const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const client = Example.client.http.make({ uri, databaseName, token })
const users = Example.client.http.group("Users", { uri, databaseName, token })

const write = client.Users.reducers.user_upsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
const read = client.Users.procedures.user_get({ userId: "u1" })
const scopedWrite = users.reducers.user_upsert({ userId: "u1", name: "Ada" })
```

For a narrower type at a consumer boundary, construct only one group view:
`Example.client.http.group("Users", { uri, databaseName, token })`. The result
contains only that group's `reducers`, `procedures`, and `httpHandlers`.

Grouped functions—including their `.raw` functions—are the exact same objects
as the flat members, so grouping has no behavioral or wire-level cost. Group
views are lazy and currently HTTP-only; WebSocket sessions remain flat.

Group ids are client property keys. Module validation rejects ids that are not
JavaScript identifiers or collide with framework/session keys (`reducers`,
`procedures`, `subscribe`, and similar) or inherited-object names such as
`constructor`.

## Raw Calls And Failures

Reducer and procedure functions expose a typed call and a `.raw` variant. The
typed call decodes declared domain errors into the error channel directly. The
raw variant preserves a `DomainCallError` wrapper so callers can distinguish a
remote declared error from transport, rejection, or decode failures.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }, { status: 404 }),
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("user_get", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Users)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* Example.client.http.Tag
  return yield* client.procedures.user_get.raw({ userId: "u1" })
}).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("DomainCallError", (failure: StdbClient.DomainCallError<unknown>) =>
    Effect.fail(failure.error),
  ),
)
```

The exported failure model is:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `CallFailure<E>` | Typed call error union: declared errors, `ConnectionLostError`, `RemoteRejectedError`, `TransportError`, or `StdbDecodeError`. |
| `RawCallFailure<E>` | Raw call error union: `DomainCallError<E>`, `ConnectionLostError`, `RemoteRejectedError`, `TransportError`, or `StdbDecodeError`. |
| `DomainCallError<E>` | Declared error preserved as a wrapper by `.raw`. |
| `ConnectionLostError` | The session was invalidated before a terminal response arrived; the call's outcome is unknown. |
| `RemoteRejectedError` | The remote side rejected the call without a decodable declared error. |
| `TransportError` | The HTTP or WebSocket transport failed before a typed response arrived. |
| `StdbDecodeError` | A response, row, event, or payload could not be decoded with the module contract. |

The lower-level `catchRawTags` helper is exported from
`effect-spacetimedb/testing` for fixture and protocol-level assertions. Public
application clients should usually handle the exported failure classes directly
or use the typed call form.

## HTTP API Base URL

Use `Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl` with `Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)` when you want a
stock Effect `HttpApiClient` over typed `post`, `put`, or `patch` routes.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/unstable/httpapi/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule
declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string

const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  return client
})
```

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/dev-publish

---
draft: false
title: Dev & Publish
description: Use the native SpacetimeDB CLI build, dev, and publish flow.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/developing" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Dev & Publish ↗</a>

Build with the native SpacetimeDB CLI. The module entry imports the host-only
compiler, imports server polyfills as a side effect, and exports the compiled
schema.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app")

export const compiled = build(Module, [])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

Publish a built bundle with the native SpacetimeDB CLI rather than a placeholder
module-path publish command:

```sh
spacetime build --module-path <moduleDir>
spacetime publish --js-path <moduleDir>/dist/bundle.js --server <url> <dbName>
```

The upstream `spacetime dev` command needs the full module path, server,
database, identity, and publish settings for your local environment; see the
[SpacetimeDB CLI docs](https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/developing) for the
dev and publish flags.

## Programmatic Dev Servers

`effect-spacetimedb/dev-server` is for tests and tools that need a temporary
local `spacetimedb-standalone` plus a published prebuilt bundle. It does not
build the module or generate clients.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import { makeDevServer } from "effect-spacetimedb/dev-server"

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const runtime = yield* makeDevServer({
    bundlePath: "dist/bundle.js",
    dbNamePrefix: "example",
  })

  yield* Effect.logInfo(
    `published ${runtime.databaseName} at ${runtime.baseUrl}`,
  )

  return runtime
})
```

The generated server bundle must include
`effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`; native `spacetime build` preserves its
side-effectful server polyfill import. Off-host tests that import server modules
also need the `spacetime:sys` stub from
`effect-spacetimedb/testing/spacetime-sys`.

effect-spacetimedb controls the authored TypeScript contract and compiled
module exports; SpacetimeDB still controls local dev, publish, runtime storage,
and the generated client runtime. The optional
[quarantined codegen path](/core-concepts/clients/codegen) bundles native output
without replacing the native generator.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/migrations

---
draft: false
title: Migrations
description: Link to SpacetimeDB migrations; effect-spacetimedb adds no migration layer.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/automatic-migrations" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Migrations ↗</a>

Migrations are a SpacetimeDB runtime concern. effect-spacetimedb does not add a
separate migration DSL or change the host migration model.

Use `Stdb.table(...)`, `Stdb.scheduledTable(...)`, and the callable builders to
declare the next module schema, then follow SpacetimeDB's migration guidance for
publishing and upgrading databases. What follows is the part of the host model
that decides whether a redeclaration of your contract can be published over a
live database.

## What Publishing Can Change In Place

Reducers, procedures, views, and HTTP handlers are not part of a migration plan
at all. Add, remove, rename, and retype them freely.

Tables are planned. `spacetime publish` computes the migration, prints it, and
asks before applying anything that disconnects clients. These changes are
automatic:

- adding a table, or removing one that holds no rows;
- adding or removing an index;
- adding or removing a unique constraint, and changing which column is the
  primary key;
- adding or removing an auto-increment sequence — rejected if existing values
  already fall inside the new sequence's range;
- flipping a table between public and private;
- appending columns **that declare a default**;
- a layout-compatible column type change: a sum may gain variants appended at
  the end as long as every existing variant keeps its name and position and the
  encoded size and alignment do not change;
- any column change at all on an event table, which holds no resident rows.

These require a fresh database (`spacetime publish --delete-data`) or the
incremental-migration pattern: removing a column, reordering columns, removing a
table that still holds rows, changing a column to a layout-incompatible type,
and adding or removing a schedule.

The whole migration runs in one transaction. If any step fails, it rolls back
and the database keeps its previous schema and its data.

## Appending A Column

A new column has to be last and has to declare a default, because the host
materializes that default into every existing row.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
    // Appended in a later version of this module.
    loginCount: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})
```

Without a default the publish is refused while the plan is computed, before the
database is touched. A default cannot be combined with `.primaryKey()`,
`.unique()`, or `.autoInc()`, so a new key column is never an appended column.
Appending rewrites every row of the table and disconnects connected clients; it
is not a metadata-only change.

## Adding A Unique Or Primary Key Constraint

Adding `.unique()` or `.primaryKey()` to a column of an already-populated table
is an automatic migration when the existing rows satisfy it. When they do not,
the migration fails and rolls back with the data intact, reporting how many
duplicate groups it found and listing the first ten offending values with their
occurrence counts. Columns are identified by position in that message, not by
name.

:::note

SpacetimeDB's own automatic-migrations page still lists this under forbidden
changes. The host has allowed it since the 2.7.0 release; the upstream page has
not caught up.

:::

## Renaming

The declared table name is both the client-facing accessor and the name the
database stores the table under, so changing it is a rename of the table itself
— remove plus add — and it fails while the table holds rows. Changing a module's
case-conversion policy rewrites every stored name the same way.

Columns are the exception worth knowing, because `.name("db_name")` pins the
database column name independently of the TypeScript field name. With the
database name pinned, renaming the field renames only the accessor, which
migrates in place.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/databases/transactions-atomicity

---
draft: false
title: Transactions & Atomicity
description: Reducer transactions, explicit procedure transactions, and retry-safe bodies.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/databases/transactions-atomicity" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Transactions & Atomicity ↗</a>

Reducers run inside the host reducer transaction and may yield `Db` directly.
Procedures and HTTP handlers open explicit transactions with `Tx` or `HttpTx`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const counter = Stdb.table("counter", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    value: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})

const Counters = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Counters")
  .add(Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("counter_inc", { params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }) }))
  .add(Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("counter_read", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(counter.row),
  }))

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(counter).add(Counters)
const { Db, Tx } = Module

const CountersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Counters", {
  counter_inc: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const db = yield* Db
    const current = yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
    yield* db.counter.id.replace({ id, value: (current?.value ?? 0) + 1 })
  }),
  counter_read: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        return yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Effect capability scopes make transaction boundaries visible in
the type system. Keep `Tx.run(...)` and `HttpTx.run(...)` bodies idempotent and
database-only; put external side effects outside the transaction body.

SpaceTimeDB owns transaction commit, abort, rollback, and optimistic-commit
retry behavior. effect-spacetimedb delegates to the native host `withTx` call; it
does not add retry logic of its own. An Effect failure inside the body aborts the
transaction. Native host abort outcomes surface as typed errors such as
`StdbUniqueAlreadyExistsError`, `StdbNoSuchRowError`, and
`StdbAutoIncOverflowError`.

HTTP handlers use `HttpTx` for the same explicit transaction boundary:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const counter = Stdb.table("counter", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    value: Stdb.u32().default(0),
  },
})

const Routes = Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make("Routes").add(
  Stdb.StdbHttp.post("counter_inc", "/counter/inc", {
    request: Schema.Struct({ id: Schema.String }),
    response: Schema.Void,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(counter).add(Routes)
const { Db, HttpTx } = Module

const RoutesLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Routes", {
  counter_inc: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* HttpTx
    yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        const current = yield* db.counter.id.find(id)
        yield* db.counter.id.replace({
          id,
          value: (current?.value ?? 0) + 1,
        })
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

See [Runtime Model](/the-effect-layer/runtime-model) for the server Effect
constraints.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/error-handling

---
draft: false
title: Error Handling
description: Model domain failures as tagged errors that cross reducer, procedure, route, and client boundaries.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/error-handling" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Error Handling ↗</a>

Declared errors are tagged errors with a namespace prefix. The namespace keeps
wire tags globally unique within a module, while each field uses a normal
`Stdb.*` value type.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_require", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
  Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("user_get", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const UserRoutes = Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make("UserRoutes").add(
  Stdb.StdbHttp.post("user_token_rotate", "/users/token/rotate", {
    request: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    response: Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Users).add(UserRoutes)

const fail = (userId: string) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    return yield* new AppErrors.UserMissing({ userId })
  })
```

Attach the error catalog with `errors:` and fail with the generated classes
directly. Declared errors are encoded on the wire with a versioned envelope, so
plain host rejection strings are not confused with domain failures.

An error can optionally declare an HTTP status with
`Stdb.error(fields, { status })`. That status applies only when the error
surfaces over an HTTP route; on the reducer and procedure (WebSocket) path there
is no HTTP response, so it is ignored.

Clients receive declared tagged errors directly from reducer and procedure
calls, and typed HTTP routes deliver the same errors through the projected
Effect `HttpApi` client:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/unstable/httpapi/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string
declare const userId: string

const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_require", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
  Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("user_get", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() })),
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const UserRoutes = Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make("UserRoutes").add(
  Stdb.StdbHttp.post("user_token_rotate", "/users/token/rotate", {
    request: Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    response: Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema,
    errors: AppErrors,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Users).add(UserRoutes)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)
const rpcClient = Example.client.http.make({ uri, databaseName, token })

const requireUser = rpcClient.reducers.user_require({ userId }).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", (error) =>
    Effect.log(`missing ${error.userId}`),
  ),
)

const findUser = rpcClient.procedures.user_get({ userId }).pipe(
  Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", () => Effect.succeed(undefined)),
)

const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const rotateToken = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  return yield* client.UserRoutes.user_token_rotate({
    payload: { userId },
  }).pipe(
    Effect.map((response) => response.token),
    Effect.catchTag("AppUserMissing", () => Effect.succeed(undefined)),
  )
})
```

Use `.raw(...)` only when you need remote rejection metadata in addition to the
decoded declared error.

A failing reducer aborts its transaction and rejects the caller's call with the
declared error's payload intact. That rejection is the only place the payload
appears: the host does not copy it into the module's server log, so
`spacetime logs` is not a channel for observing which declared error aborted a
transaction. Log deliberately from the handler when an operator needs to see it.

Subscription and stream APIs report subscription, transport, invalidation, and
row-decode failures. They do not carry declared domain errors because declared
errors are emitted by reducer, procedure, and typed HTTP route calls.

Declared errors are Effect failures. Defects remain defects, and
plain host rejection strings are kept separate from decoded domain failures.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/http-handlers

---
draft: false
title: HTTP Handlers
description: Add typed and raw server-to-server HTTP handlers to a module.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/http-handlers" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: HTTP Handlers ↗</a>

HTTP routes are server-to-server routes, not caller-authenticated reducers. Their
context exposes the module database identity, timestamp, HTTP request data,
randomness, UUID helpers, and transaction-scoped DB access. It does not expose a
caller `sender`, caller identity, or connection id.

Declare routes in an `StdbHttpGroup`. Typed routes provide `request` and
`response` schemas; raw routes omit them and work directly with `Request` and
`SyncResponse`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const tokenRotation = Stdb.table("token_rotation", {
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    token: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const RotateTokenInput = Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema
const RotateTokenOutput = Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema

const Webhooks = Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make("Webhooks")
  .prefix("/webhooks")
  .add(Stdb.StdbHttp.post("stripe_webhook", "/stripe"))
  .add(
    Stdb.StdbHttp.post("rotate_token", "/rotate", {
      request: RotateTokenInput,
      response: RotateTokenOutput,
    }),
  )

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app")
  .addTables(tokenRotation)
  .add(Webhooks)
const { HttpTx, Db } = Module

const WebhooksLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Webhooks", {
  stripe_webhook: (request) =>
    Effect.succeed(new Stdb.SyncResponse(request.text(), { status: 202 })),
  rotate_token: (args) =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const tx = yield* HttpTx
      return yield* tx.run(
        Effect.gen(function* () {
          const db = yield* Db
          const row = yield* db.token_rotation.userId.replace({
            userId: args.userId,
            token: `token:${args.userId}`,
          })
          return { token: row.token }
        }),
      )
    }),
})
```

Use raw routes for GET or HEAD, query strings, custom auth headers, webhooks, and
non-JSON bodies. Keep external side effects outside HTTP transaction bodies, just
as you would for procedures.

These are inbound routes the module serves. They are unrelated to the
`[module-http]` server setting, which governs requests a module *makes* — see
[Procedures](/core-concepts/functions/procedures).

effect-spacetimedb uses `StdbHttpGroup` plus
`StdbBuilder.group(...)` instead of exporting handler functions directly. Typed
`post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can also be projected to an Effect `HttpApi`.

## Project Typed Routes To HttpApi

Typed `post`, `put`, and `patch` routes can also be projected into a canonical
Effect `HttpApi`. The STDB HTTP group becomes the `HttpApiClient` property key,
and the route name becomes the typed endpoint method.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as HttpClient from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClient"
import * as HttpClientRequest from "effect/unstable/http/HttpClientRequest"
import * as HttpApiClient from "effect/unstable/httpapi/HttpApiClient"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const uri: string
declare const databaseName: string
declare const token: string
declare const userId: string

const RotateTokenInput = Stdb.struct({ userId: Stdb.string() }).schema
const RotateTokenOutput = Stdb.struct({ token: Stdb.string() }).schema

const Webhooks = Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make("Webhooks").add(
  Stdb.StdbHttp.post("rotate_token", "/rotate", {
    request: RotateTokenInput,
    response: RotateTokenOutput,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").add(Webhooks)
const api = Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const client = yield* HttpApiClient.make(api, {
    baseUrl: Stdb.httpApiBaseUrl({ uri, databaseName }),
    transformClient: HttpClient.mapRequest(
      HttpClientRequest.bearerToken(token),
    ),
  })

  const response = yield* client.Webhooks.rotate_token({
    payload: { userId },
  })

  return response.token
})
```

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/lifecycle

---
draft: false
title: Lifecycle
description: Declare init, clientConnected, and clientDisconnected hooks.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/lifecycle" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Lifecycle ↗</a>

Lifecycle hooks can be declared in the module config and implemented with
`StdbBuilder.lifecycle(...)`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Lifecycle = {
  init: Stdb.StdbFn.init(),
  clientConnected: Stdb.StdbFn.clientConnected(),
  clientDisconnected: Stdb.StdbFn.clientDisconnected(),
}

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app", {
  lifecycle: Lifecycle,
})
const { ReducerCtx } = Module

const LifecycleLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.lifecycle(Module, {
  // Runs once when the module is first published.
  init: () => Effect.log("module initialized"),
  // clientConnected / clientDisconnected run as the joining or leaving client,
  // so ReducerCtx identifies who it was.
  clientConnected: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    yield* Effect.log(`client connected: ${ctx.connectionId}`)
  }),
  clientDisconnected: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    yield* Effect.log(`client disconnected: ${ctx.connectionId}`)
  }),
})
```

Lifecycle hooks are first-class module declarations, not loose
exports. At most one `init`, `clientConnected`, and `clientDisconnected` hook
can be present in a built module, and handlers are checked against the module's
Effect capability scope.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/procedures

---
draft: false
title: Procedures
description: Declare read-returning callables and run mutations inside explicit transactions.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/procedures" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Procedures ↗</a>

Procedures are declared in callable groups with params and a return value type.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.procedure("user_get", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }),
    returns: Stdb.option(user.row),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db, Tx } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", {
  user_get: Effect.fn(function* ({ id }) {
    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        return yield* db.user.id.find(id)
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Procedure handlers cannot yield `Db` directly. Use the module's
`Tx` runner and keep transaction bodies pure database work because the native
runtime may retry them after optimistic commit conflicts.

## Outbound HTTP

A procedure is the only place a module can make an outbound request. Yield the
module's `Http` accessor outside any transaction — the host refuses a request
while a transaction is open, so fetch first, then open the transaction that
records the result.

```ts
const { Http, Tx, Db } = Module

const syncLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Sync", {
  sync_profile: Effect.fn(function* ({ userId }) {
    const http = yield* Http
    const response = yield* http.fetch(`https://example.test/users/${userId}`)
    const profile = yield* http.json<{ readonly name: string }>(response)

    const tx = yield* Tx
    return yield* tx.run(
      Effect.gen(function* () {
        const db = yield* Db
        yield* db.user.userId.replace({ userId, name: profile.name })
      }),
    )
  }),
})
```

Failures arrive as `StdbHostCallError` in the error channel, tagged with the
operation (`http.fetch`, `http.json`, and so on).

Two host policies decide whether a request is allowed at all, and both are the
operator's, not the module's:

- **Egress filtering.** Requests to loopback, link-local, and private or
  otherwise special-purpose addresses are refused — `127.0.0.1`, `10/8`,
  `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, the IPv6 equivalents, and the rest of the
  special-purpose registry. Ordinary server builds enforce this; only a
  purpose-built test binary relaxes it for loopback. A module cannot reach a
  service on its own host or elsewhere inside a private network. Where a
  hostname resolves to both a blocked and a routable address, the routable one
  is used.
- **A global off switch.** A standalone operator can disable module-originated
  HTTP entirely with `[module-http] enabled = false` in the server's
  `config.toml`. It defaults to enabled and takes a server restart to change.
  With it off, every request fails with `module outbound HTTP requests are
  disabled`.

Requests time out after 30 seconds unless you pass a shorter one, and the host
clamps any requested timeout to 180 seconds.

## Scheduling

Scheduled reducers and procedures are declared with the callable group API and
backed by a scheduled table. The scheduled endpoint receives
`{ data: table.row }`; insert future work with the generated table
`.schedule(row)` helper from a reducer or transaction body.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const reminderSchedule = Stdb.scheduledTable("reminderSchedule", {
  columns: {
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Reminders = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Reminders").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.scheduledProcedure("reminderFire", {
    table: reminderSchedule,
    allowExternalCallers: false,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app")
  .addTables(reminderSchedule)
  .add(Reminders)

const { Db } = Module

const RemindersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Reminders", {
  reminderFire: Effect.fn(function* ({ data }) {
    yield* Effect.logInfo(`reminder: ${data.note}`)
  }),
})

const enqueueReminder = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const db = yield* Db
  yield* db.reminderSchedule.schedule({
    scheduledAt: Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval("5 minutes"),
    note: "wake up",
  })
})
```

Use `Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval(...)` for persistent re-fire rows,
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.at(...)` for one-shot absolute times,
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.after(ctx.timestamp, duration)` for one-shot relative work, and
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.nextCron(cron, ctx.timestamp)` for cron-derived one-shots.
See [Scheduled Tables](/core-concepts/tables/scheduled-tables) for the table
side of the contract, the host's dispatch semantics, and why a scheduled
procedure that does external work between transactions has to claim its work
rows in the transaction that selects them.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/reducer-context

---
draft: false
title: Reducer Context
description: Read sender, timestamp, deterministic randomness, and scoped mutation context.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers/reducer-context" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Reducer Context ↗</a>

Reducer context is an Effect service yielded from the assembled module.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const audit = Stdb.table("audit", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    sender: Stdb.identity(),
    message: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Audit = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Audit").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("audit_write", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ message: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(audit).add(Audit)
const { Db, ReducerCtx } = Module

const AuditLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Audit", {
  audit_write: Effect.fn(function* ({ message }) {
    const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
    const db = yield* Db
    yield* db.audit.insert({
      id: 0n,
      sender: ctx.sender,
      message,
    })
  }),
})
```

`ReducerCtx` exposes the sender identity, authenticated sender metadata,
timestamp, connection id, deterministic random stream, UUID helpers, and the
same writable `db` view available through `Db`.

effect-spacetimedb exposes context as scoped services rather than a positional
argument: `ReducerCtx` for reducers, `TxCtx` inside explicit transaction bodies,
and `MutationCtx` for helpers that must work in both scopes.

:::caution

Reducers are deterministic synchronous host calls. `async`/Promises, timers,
microtasks, global `Math.random`, and wall-clock reads such as `Date.now()` or
no-argument `new Date()` throw typed errors. Use `Random.*` from
`effect/Random`, context randomness, and the call timestamp instead. See
[Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism).

:::


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/reducers

---
draft: false
title: Reducers
description: Declare reducers in callable groups and implement them with Effect handlers.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/reducers" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Reducers ↗</a>

The authoring surface follows one shape: endpoints become groups, groups become
a module, handlers implement those groups, and the completed module is built.

## Keep Contracts And Implementations Separate

Contracts are imported by the module. Implementations import the assembled
module so they can use its typed accessors. Keeping those directions separate
avoids runtime import cycles.

```text
schema.ts             shared Effect schemas and value types
tables/users.ts       table declarations
users/contract.ts     StdbGroup.make().add(...)
module.ts             StdbModule.make(...).addTables(...).add(...)
users/live.ts         StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", ...)
index.ts              build(Module, [...])
```

## Assemble The Module Once

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: { id: Stdb.string().primaryKey() },
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_upsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

export const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app")
  .addTables(user)
  .add(Users)

export const { Db, Tx, ReadonlyDb, From, ReducerCtx, ProcedureCtx, ViewCtx } = Module
```

Destructure accessors from the assembled module and use those exact accessors in
handlers. They are typed against the module's tables and scopes.

## Implement Groups By Name

`StdbBuilder.group(Module, "GroupName", handlers)` takes a record whose keys
match endpoint names in the group. The builder checks that every endpoint is
implemented exactly once.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: { id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(), name: Stdb.string() },
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_upsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", {
  user_upsert: Effect.fn(function* (args) {
    const db = yield* Db
    yield* db.user.id.replace(args)
  }),
})
```

Reducers are declared as data with `StdbFn.reducer(...)` and
implemented later with Effect handlers. Reducer handlers may yield `Db`,
`ReducerCtx`, and `MutationCtx`; transaction boundaries remain the host reducer
call.

:::caution

Reducers are deterministic synchronous host calls. Promises, `async`, timers,
microtasks, global `Math.random`, and wall-clock reads such as `Date.now()` or
no-argument `new Date()` throw typed runtime errors. Use `Random.*` from
`effect/Random`, `ctx.random`, and the call timestamp instead. See
[Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism).

:::

Lifecycle hooks use `StdbBuilder.lifecycle(Module, handlers)`. HTTP route groups
use the same `StdbBuilder.group` shape as callable groups.

## Build The Native Export

```ts
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

export const compiled = build(Module, [UsersLive])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

When storing implementations before building, keep the array readonly:

```ts
export const LiveGroups = [UsersLive] as const
export const compiled = build(Module, LiveGroups)
```

:::note

If handlers require custom services, pass a runtime layer to
`build`. Built-in SpaceTimeDB capabilities are supplied by the runtime.

:::

```ts
import * as Context from "effect/Context"
import * as Layer from "effect/Layer"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

// A custom capability your handlers need — here, injected config.
class AppConfig extends Context.Tag("AppConfig")<
  AppConfig,
  { readonly welcomeMessage: string }
>() {}

// Handlers read it with `const config = yield* AppConfig`. Because a handler
// requires AppConfig, build now asks for its runtime layer.
const AppConfigLive = Layer.succeed(AppConfig, { welcomeMessage: "welcome" })

export const compiled = build(Module, [UsersLive], { runtime: AppConfigLive })
```


---

# Source: /core-concepts/functions/views

---
draft: false
title: Views
description: Declare sender and anonymous views with typed read-only access.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/functions/views" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Views ↗</a>

Views are callable group endpoints with return value types. Sender views use
`StdbFn.view(...)`; anonymous views use `StdbFn.anonymousView(...)`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users")
  .add(Stdb.StdbFn.view("self_user", { returns: Stdb.option(user.row) }))
  .add(Stdb.StdbFn.anonymousView("all_users", { returns: Stdb.array(user.row) }))

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { ReadonlyDb, ViewCtx } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", {
  self_user: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const ctx = yield* ViewCtx
    const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
    return yield* db.user.id.find(String(ctx.sender))
  }),
  all_users: Effect.fn(function* () {
    const db = yield* ReadonlyDb
    return yield* db.user.toArray()
  }),
})
```

Views are read-only Effect handlers. Sender views may yield
`ViewCtx`; anonymous views may yield `AnonymousViewCtx`. Both may yield
`ReadonlyDb` and `From`.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/subscriptions

---
draft: false
title: Subscriptions
description: Use scoped WebSocket sessions, table targets, and event-table streams safely.
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/subscriptions/semantics" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Subscriptions ↗</a>

Subscriptions are scoped native resources. A session can subscribe to public
tables and event tables, then release each subscription when the scope exits or
the handle is unsubscribed.

```ts
const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const session = yield* Example.client.ws.Session

  yield* session.subscribe(Example.targets.allPublicTables())
  yield* session.streamEventTable("presenceEvent").pipe(Stream.runDrain)
})
```

Each subscribe call opens its own native SpacetimeDB query set on the session
connection. `allPublicTables()` remains one native multi-query subscription.

The wrapper intentionally follows the native TypeScript SDK model:

- `session.subscribe(target)` opens one native subscription for that target.
- `tableGroup(keys).subscribe` opens one native subscription per table key.
- `streamTable`, `streamRows`, `streamTableWithContext`,
  `streamTableEvents`, and `streamEventTable` each open the subscription needed
  for that stream.
- `allPublicTables()` remains one native multi-query subscription.

If two consumers subscribe to the same table or event table, they own two native
query sets. The wrapper does not add query-key APIs or client-side
deduplication on top of the native SDK.

## Streams

Persistent-table streams use bounded callback queues by default and should be
treated as invalidation signals: re-read the authoritative session cache when a
change arrives. Event-table streams are raw event feeds and are unbounded unless
you opt into a bounded buffer and accept lossy overflow behavior.

The session stream helper family covers the common shapes:

| Helper | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `streamTable(key, options?)` | Persistent-table insert/update/delete signals. |
| `streamRows(key)` | Initial snapshot followed by cache snapshots after table changes. |
| `tableGroup(keys, options?)` | Multi-table snapshot group with `subscribe`, `readSnapshot`, and `changes`. |
| `streamTableEvents(key, options?)` | Persistent-table changes with decoded `StdbEventContext`. |
| `streamEventTable(key, options?)` | Event-table insert feed. |
| `streamTarget(target, options?)` | Stream a projected subscription target. |

Persistent-table streams accept `{ buffer: { bufferSize, strategy } }`, where
`strategy` is `"sliding"` or `"dropping"`. The default is a bounded sliding
queue sized for cache invalidation signals. Event-table streams accept
`{ buffer: { bufferSize } }`; overflowing that buffer fails the stream with
`EventTableStreamOverflowError` rather than silently dropping events.

Event tables use native delivery semantics. Every live native query set that
covers an event can deliver that event, so subscribe once at an app state
boundary and fan out from that stream when a domain needs one event-processing
path.

Persistent table subscriptions populate the native connection cache. The cache
merges row coverage across live query sets, so snapshot reads through generated
client caches, `streamRows(key)`, and `tableGroup(keys).readSnapshot` always
read the connection-owned table state rather than a wrapper-local copy. A
transaction applies atomically before callbacks fire, so snapshot reads taken
from callbacks observe the post-transaction cache.

`tableGroup(keys).changes` emits an initial snapshot and then burst-coalesced
snapshots by re-reading the generated client's authoritative cache. Native SDK
callbacks for one server message are dispatched synchronously, so a transaction
burst normally lands in one drain batch and produces one snapshot. If the
consumer falls behind, several bursts can coalesce into one later snapshot; the
emission still re-reads the post-apply cache and converges to current state.

## Event Context

`streamTableEvents` decodes native generated-client event metadata into
`StdbEventContext`. Use `decodeStdbEventContext` from
`effect-spacetimedb/client` when you are working with lower-level generated
callbacks yourself.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as StdbClient from "effect-spacetimedb/client"

declare const rawContext: unknown

const decoded = StdbClient.decodeStdbEventContext(rawContext).pipe(
  Effect.map((context): StdbClient.StdbEventContextType => context),
)
```

## Failure Propagation

Subscription setup failures are routed into the stream queue explicitly so
rejected subscriptions, invalidated connections, and transport errors do not
turn into streams that simply never emit.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/access-permissions

---
draft: false
title: Access Permissions
description: Public table visibility, and the unsupported RLS surface.
sidebar:
  order: 8
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/access-permissions" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Access Permissions ↗</a>

effect-spacetimedb supports table-level public visibility:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const publicUser = Stdb.table("public_user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
  },
})

const privateAudit = Stdb.table("private_audit", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Row-level security / `clientVisibilityFilter` is not supported. Use private
tables plus reducers, procedures, views, or HTTP handlers to expose scoped data
intentionally.

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/auto-increment

---
draft: false
title: Auto-Increment
description: Use auto-increment primary keys and generated schedule ids.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/auto-increment" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Auto-Increment ↗</a>

Auto-increment is column metadata on a primary key. Chain `.primaryKey()` before
`.autoInc()` so the declaration satisfies SpacetimeDB's host rules.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const issue = Stdb.table("issue", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    title: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Scheduled tables derive their auto-increment schedule id for you:

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const reminderSchedule = Stdb.scheduledTable("reminder_schedule", {
  columns: {
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

effect-spacetimedb validates auto-increment at declaration time:
`.autoInc()` without `.primaryKey()` throws, and defaults cannot be combined with
primary keys or auto-increment columns.

`.autoInc()` is narrower than `.primaryKey()`: only the integer widths carry a
sequence. A string, identity, UUID, timestamp, or sum primary key is a legal key
but rejects `.autoInc()` — allocate those values in the handler.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/column-types

---
draft: false
title: Column Types
description: Declare typed tables, indexes, constraints, rows, and reusable value types.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/column-types" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Column Types ↗</a>

Tables are declared with `Stdb.table(name, options)`. Bind each table to a
variable so its `row` value type, column metadata, index metadata, and generated
accessor types can flow through the module.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId"))
const ShortString = Stdb.string(Schema.String.pipe(Schema.minLength(1)))

export const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string(UserId).primaryKey(),
    name: ShortString,
  },
})

export const membership = Stdb.table("membership", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    tenant_id: ShortString,
    email: ShortString,
  },
  indexes: (c) => [Stdb.index("membership_email_tenant_idx", [c.email, c.tenant_id])],
  constraints: (c) => [Stdb.unique("membership_tenant_email_unique", [c.tenant_id, c.email])],
})
```

effect-spacetimedb wraps Effect schemas in `Stdb.*` value types, then uses those
value types consistently for table columns, reducer/procedure params, view
returns, and declared errors.

Any value type can be a column. Which ones can carry a key or an index is a
narrower question: see [Constraints](/core-concepts/tables/constraints) for the
primary-key and unique-capable types and [Indexes](/core-concepts/tables/indexes)
for the indexable ones. `Stdb.enum(...)` and `Stdb.sum(...)` columns qualify for
both.

## Value-Type Pattern

Use a plain Effect schema as the domain source of truth, then wrap it at
SpaceTimeDB declaration boundaries:

```ts
const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId"))

Stdb.string(UserId) // table columns, params, returns, and declared error fields
```

Keep reusable `Stdb.*` aliases for generic non-branded values, such as a
length-limited string used in many columns. For custom codecs, use
`Stdb.custom(schema, { type })` so the SpaceTimeDB lowering is explicit.

For the full helper catalog, including integer widths, native timestamp/UUID
values, and transport codecs, see [Value Types](/the-effect-layer/value-types).

## Column Names And Row Types

Use `.name("db_name")` on a value type when the database column name should
differ from the TypeScript field name.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string().name("user_id").primaryKey(),
    displayName: Stdb.string().name("display_name"),
  },
})

type UserRow = Stdb.TableRow<typeof user>

const UserRow = Stdb.rowType(user)
const SameUserRow = user.row
```

`Stdb.rowType(table)` and `table.row` are the reusable value type for a full row;
`Stdb.TableRow<typeof table>` is the authored TypeScript row type.

## Optionality

`Stdb.option(T)` means the value is present but may be `undefined`.
`Stdb.optional(T)` and `.optional()` mean the field or table column may be
omitted. Both lower to SATS `option<T>` where structs are materialized, but they
produce different TypeScript property shapes.

See [Value-Type Design](/the-effect-layer/value-type-design) and
[Option vs Optional](/the-effect-layer/option-vs-optional) for the Effect-native
typing details.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/constraints

---
draft: false
title: Constraints
description: Declare primary keys and unique constraints with value-type metadata.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/constraints" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Constraints ↗</a>

Primary keys and single-column unique constraints are declared on the column
value type. Multi-column unique constraints are declared in the table's
`constraints` callback so column names stay type-checked.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const membership = Stdb.table("membership", {
  public: false,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    tenantId: Stdb.string(),
    email: Stdb.string(),
    externalId: Stdb.string().unique(),
  },
  constraints: (columns) => [
    Stdb.unique("membership_tenant_email_unique", [
      columns.tenantId,
      columns.email,
    ]),
  ],
})
```

Column-level `.unique()` also creates the backing index when one
is not already implied by a primary key or explicit index. A default value cannot
be combined with a unique constraint because SpacetimeDB would materialize the
same default for more than one row.

## Key-Capable Column Types

A key column has to be something the host can order and compare: the integer
widths, `bool`, `string`, `Stdb.bigint()`, `Stdb.identity()`,
`Stdb.connectionId()`, `Stdb.timestamp()`, `Stdb.timeDuration()`,
`Stdb.uuid()`, and any `Stdb.enum(...)` or `Stdb.sum(...)`. A sum keys on its
whole encoded value, so a payload variant is a distinct key per payload:
`{ tag: "Retrying", value: 7 }` and `{ tag: "Retrying", value: 9 }` are two
rows under a sum primary key.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Status = Stdb.sum({
  Ready: Stdb.unit(),
  Retrying: Stdb.u32(),
})

const progress = Stdb.table("progress", {
  columns: {
    status: Status.primaryKey(),
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})
```

Arrays, structs, `Stdb.f32()`/`f64()`, and numeric `Stdb.literal(...)` (which
lowers to `f64`) are rejected as primary keys at declaration time. `.autoInc()`
stays narrower still: it applies only to the integer widths, so a sum, string,
or identity primary key cannot be auto-incremented.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/default-values

---
draft: false
title: Default Values
description: Attach native SpaceTimeDB column defaults to value types.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/default-values" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Default Values ↗</a>

Column defaults are declared with `.default(value)` on a value type.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const profile = Stdb.table("profile", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    displayName: Stdb.string().default("anonymous"),
    score: Stdb.u32().default(0),
    subscribed: Stdb.bool().default(false),
  },
})
```

Defaults use the authored TypeScript value for the wrapped
`Stdb.*` value type. The library rejects defaults on primary keys,
auto-increment columns, unique columns, and unsupported native metadata shapes.

A default is also what makes a column appendable to a table that already holds
rows — see [Migrations](/core-concepts/databases/migrations).

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/event-tables

---
draft: false
title: Event Tables
description: Declare event tables and subscribe to event-table streams safely.
sidebar:
  order: 7
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/event-tables" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Event Tables ↗</a>

Event tables use the same `Stdb.table(...)` builder with `event: true`.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stream from "effect/Stream"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const presenceEvent = Stdb.table("presenceEvent", {
  public: true,
  event: true,
  columns: {
    userId: Stdb.string(),
    kind: Stdb.literal("joined", "left"),
  },
})

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("presence", {}).addTables(presenceEvent)
const Example = Stdb.project(Module)

const program = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const session = yield* Example.client.ws.Session
  yield* session.streamEventTable("presenceEvent").pipe(
    Stream.runForEach((event) =>
      Effect.log(`presence ${event.row.userId} ${event.row.kind}`),
    ),
  )
})
```

effect-spacetimedb separates public persistent table targets
from public event-table targets in `Stdb.project(...).targets`. Use
`Example.targets.eventTables.presenceEvent` for direct target subscriptions and
`streamEventTable("presenceEvent")` for insert-only event streams.

Event tables use native delivery semantics: an event is delivered once for each
live native query set that covers it. If an application needs exactly one
event-processing path, subscribe once at the app state boundary and fan out from
that Effect stream or Atom rather than opening duplicate event-table streams in
several consumers.

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/file-storage" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: File Storage ↗</a>

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/indexes

---
draft: false
title: Indexes
description: Declare btree, hash, and direct indexes from table columns.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/indexes" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Indexes ↗</a>

Single-column indexes can live on the column. Composite indexes live in the
table's `indexes` callback.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const playerScore = Stdb.table("player_score", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.u64().primaryKey().autoInc(),
    playerId: Stdb.string().index("hash"),
    score: Stdb.u32().index("direct"),
    season: Stdb.string(),
  },
  indexes: (columns) => [
    Stdb.index("player_score_season_score_idx", [
      columns.season,
      columns.score,
    ], { algorithm: "btree" }),
  ],
})
```

effect-spacetimedb accepts the native algorithms
`"btree"`, `"hash"`, and `"direct"` at both declaration sites. `hash` indexes
are point-only; `direct` indexes are range-capable.

## Indexable Column Types

`btree` and `hash` index any column type the host can key, including
`Stdb.enum(...)` and payload-carrying `Stdb.sum(...)` columns. A unit-variant
enum is keyed by its variant tag; a payload-carrying sum is keyed by its whole
encoded value, so `{ tag: "Chunk", value: 4 }` and `{ tag: "Chunk", value: 5 }`
are two different keys.

`direct` is the exception. It indexes exactly one column, and only `u8`, `u16`,
`u32`, `u64`, or a unit-variant enum.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const Kind = Stdb.enum("Ping", "Chunk")

const marker = Stdb.table("marker", {
  columns: {
    kind: Kind.index("btree"),
    seq: Stdb.u32(),
  },
  indexes: (columns) => [
    Stdb.index("marker_kind_seq_idx", [columns.kind, columns.seq], {
      algorithm: "btree",
    }),
  ],
})
```

## Composite Lookups

A composite btree index is read through the accessor named after the index. Pass
a tuple of index-column values: either a leading prefix of the columns or the
full width. The last value you supply may be a range; every column before it is
matched for equality.

```ts
// Equality on both columns: a point lookup.
yield* db.marker.marker_kind_seq_idx.filterToArray([{ tag: "Chunk" }, 7])

// Equality on `kind`, range over `seq` — a range in the final column of a
// full-width tuple is a range scan, not a point lookup.
yield* db.marker.marker_kind_seq_idx.filterToArray([
  { tag: "Chunk" },
  { from: { tag: "included", value: 1 }, to: { tag: "excluded", value: 9 } },
])

// A one-column prefix scans every `seq` under that `kind`.
yield* db.marker.marker_kind_seq_idx.filterToArray([{ tag: "Chunk" }])
```

A single-column index takes the bare value or a bare `{ from, to }` range
instead of a tuple. Bounds are `{ tag: "included" | "excluded", value }` or
`{ tag: "unbounded" }`, and `deleteAll(...)` accepts the same inputs as
`filterToArray(...)`.


---

# Source: /core-concepts/tables/performance

---
draft: false
title: Performance
description: Link to SpacetimeDB table-performance docs; effect-spacetimedb has no extra runtime semantics.
sidebar:
  order: 10
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/performance" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Performance ↗</a>

Table performance is a SpacetimeDB runtime concern. effect-spacetimedb exposes
the native index algorithms through `.index(...)` and `Stdb.index(...)`, but it
does not change the host query planner or storage semantics.

For authoring syntax, see [Indexes](/core-concepts/tables/indexes).
