# Source: /core-concepts/tables/scheduled-tables

---
draft: false
title: Scheduled Tables
description: Use scheduled tables and scheduled reducers or procedures.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

<a class="upstream-doc" href="https://spacetimedb.com/docs/tables/schedule-tables" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">SpacetimeDB: Scheduled Tables ↗</a>

Scheduled tables are private by default and reserve `scheduledId` and
`scheduledAt`. A scheduled endpoint receives `{ data: table.row }`.

`Stdb.scheduledTable(name, options)` auto-injects two columns before user
columns:

- `scheduledId`: a `u64().primaryKey().autoInc()` column with native column name
  `scheduled_id`.
- `scheduledAt`: a `ScheduleAt` column with native column name `scheduled_at`.

Authors cannot also declare `scheduledId`, `scheduledAt`, `scheduled_id`, or
`scheduled_at`; the constructor rejects those reserved names. A custom
`scheduledId` value type may be supplied through `options.scheduledId`, but it
must still be a `u64` value type and is still marked primary-key and auto-inc.

Scheduled tables default to `public: false`, the same local default as
`Stdb.table(...)`, and they honor an explicit `public: true`. User columns are
spread directly into the table shape after the injected scheduler columns; there
is no `{ data }` wrapper in the table row shape.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const reminderSchedule = Stdb.scheduledTable("reminderSchedule", {
  columns: {
    note: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Reminders = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Reminders").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.scheduledProcedure("reminderFire", {
    table: reminderSchedule,
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app")
  .addTables(reminderSchedule)
  .add(Reminders)

const RemindersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Reminders", {
  reminderFire: Effect.fn(function* ({ data }) {
    yield* Effect.log(`reminder: ${data.note}`)
  }),
})
```

To seed schedule rows inside a reducer or transaction body, use the generated
`.schedule(...)` helper. It fills the auto-increment sentinel for you.

```ts
yield* db.reminderSchedule.schedule({
  scheduledAt: Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval("5 minutes"),
  note: "wake up",
})
```

| Schedule form | Host behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Stdb.ScheduleAt.at(...)` or `after(...)` | One-shot row. Reducers consume it after execution; procedures consume it before, so a scheduled procedure can no longer find or update its own row. |
| `Stdb.ScheduleAt.interval(...)` | Row persists and re-fires until deleted. |

`Interval` covers plain re-fire spacing. Reach for self-rescheduling one-shot
rows when the target is a wall-clock or cron alignment an interval cannot
express: handle a `Time` row, insert the next one with
`Stdb.ScheduleAt.nextCron(cron, ctx.timestamp)` or `at(...)`, then return.

`Stdb.scheduledTable(...)` creates the reserved
`scheduled_id`/`scheduled_at` columns and `StdbFn.scheduledReducer(...)` or
`StdbFn.scheduledProcedure(...)` binds exactly one typed handler to the table.
The binding is registered on the function, which is where SpacetimeDB expects
it; the table itself carries no schedule option.

## Host Scheduling Semantics

These are SpacetimeDB host behaviours, not something this library adds.

**Dispatch is concurrent.** The scheduler does not wait for one due function to
finish before dispatching the next, so a slow scheduled procedure does not
delay unrelated scheduled work. Execution is bounded further down: scheduled
reducers share the module's single reducer lane and still run one at a time,
serialized with client-invoked reducers, while scheduled procedures take an
instance from a bounded pool — one per available CPU by default — and genuinely
run in parallel.

**Already-expired work has no order.** When several schedules are past due at
once, after a restart, a backlog, or an overrunning run, they are not guaranteed
to run in `scheduled_at` order. Never encode ordering between two schedule rows:
chain them, or carry an explicit sequence number in the row.

**A row does not normally overlap itself.** Each row is an independent schedule
identified by its `scheduledId`, and the host does not queue that row's next
invocation until the current one has returned. Two different rows in the same
table are separate schedules and may run at the same time. The exception is
re-arming: writing a schedule row registers its timer entry immediately, so a
procedure that updates its own row to an already-due time can be re-entered
while it is still running. Treat self-exclusion as the normal case, never as a
mutual-exclusion primitive.

**Intervals do not drift.** The next fire time is the previous *intended* time
plus the interval, not the time the last run started or finished, so timer
jitter and slow runs never accumulate. Ticks missed while the database was busy
or down are skipped rather than replayed back to back. The first fire of a newly
inserted `Interval` row is one interval away, not immediate.

**A scheduled reducer is still one transaction.** Its whole body commits or
rolls back atomically, exactly like a client-invoked reducer. For a one-shot
row, the host's deletion of that row is a separate transaction committed
immediately afterwards — subscribers see two updates — and it happens whether
the reducer succeeded or failed. Failed invocations are logged and never
retried; re-insert a schedule row from the handler if retry is part of the
domain.

## Scheduled Procedures Must Claim Their Work

A procedure has no ambient transaction: each `Tx.run(...)` is its own
transaction, and external work such as an HTTP call necessarily happens between
two of them. The host holds nothing across that gap — no row locks, no snapshot,
no exclusion. Combined with concurrent dispatch, a procedure that selects
pending rows in one transaction, calls out, and marks them done in a later
transaction will hand the same rows to a second invocation that starts in the
window between the two.

Claim the work in the same transaction that selects it: flip a status column, or
stamp an attempt id and a lease expiry, so the selecting transaction is what
makes those rows invisible to everyone else. Do the external call afterwards and
record its outcome against that claim.

Keep transaction bodies idempotent and free of captured mutable state for the
same reason procedures generally require it: the runtime may re-run a
transaction body after a commit conflict.

## Validation Boundaries

The TypeScript DSL rejects raw schemas in SATS positions at compile time by
requiring opaque value types. Cross-object module invariants are validated by
`validateModule` / `Stdb.validate`:

| Invariant | Compile-time | Runtime validation diagnostic |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Raw Effect schema in a SATS position | Yes | `UnsupportedTypeDescriptor` remains as a malformed-spec fallback |
| Duplicate table/view relation names | No | `DuplicateRelationName` |
| Duplicate reducer/procedure/HTTP/view/lifecycle export names | No | `DuplicateCallableName` |
| Reserved `__http_router__` export name | No | `DuplicateCallableName` |
| Non-canonical declared names under canonical naming policy | No | `NonCanonicalDeclaredName` |
| Reserved declared error tags | No | `ReservedDeclaredErrorTag` |
| Duplicate declared error tags | No | `DuplicateDeclaredErrorTag` |
| String literal authored/generated-client tag collisions | No | `LiteralTagCollision` |

Broad cross-group uniqueness checks stay in runtime validation because lifting
large cross-object comparisons into the type system can hit TypeScript
instantiation-depth limits. Smaller bounded checks, such as reserved names and
casing policy, are better candidates for future compile-time feedback.


---

# Source: /getting-started

---
draft: false
title: Getting Started
description: Install effect-spacetimedb, write a minimal module, build it, and generate a client.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

import { TabItem, Tabs } from "@astrojs/starlight/components";

`effect-spacetimedb` is an Effect-first authoring layer for SpaceTimeDB modules.
You describe the module once, implement handlers with scoped Effect services,
then build native module exports and generated clients from the same contract.

## Install

<Tabs syncKey="package-manager">
  <TabItem label="npm">

    ```sh
    npm install effect-spacetimedb effect@4.0.0-rc.117 spacetimedb@2.10.1
    ```

  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="pnpm">

    ```sh
    pnpm add effect-spacetimedb effect@4.0.0-rc.117 spacetimedb@2.10.1
    ```

  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="bun">

    ```sh
    bun add effect-spacetimedb effect@4.0.0-rc.117 spacetimedb@2.10.1
    ```

  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

:::caution[Version match]

The SpaceTimeDB CLI version must match the `spacetimedb` package version your
project depends on — `spacetime build` and `spacetime generate` read a
version-specific module format:

```sh
spacetime --version   # must match your installed `spacetimedb` package
```

If several CLI versions are installed, make sure the matching `spacetime` is the
one on your `PATH`, or invoke it by full path in your build scripts.

:::

## Minimal Module

The same module — a `user` table and a `user_upsert` reducer — in
effect-spacetimedb and in the native SpaceTimeDB SDK:

<Tabs syncKey="impl">
  <TabItem label="effect-spacetimedb">

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"
import { build } from "effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler"

// Branded + validated id. In the native SDK this column is just `string`.
const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(
  Schema.minLength(1),
  Schema.maxLength(64),
  Schema.brand("UserId"),
)

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    // The Effect schema IS the column's value type, so the brand and the
    // length validation flow through to handlers and generated clients.
    id: Stdb.string(UserId).primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

// camelCase names lower to snake_case on the wire (userUpsert -> user_upsert).
const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("userUpsert", {
    // Params are validated by the same schema; the native SDK accepts any string.
    params: Stdb.struct({
      id: Stdb.string(UserId),
      name: Stdb.string(),
    }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db } = Module

const UsersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", {
  userUpsert: (args) =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const db = yield* Db
      yield* db.user.insert(args)
    }),
})

export const compiled = build(Module, [UsersLive])
export const ModuleExports = compiled.exportGroup()
export default compiled.schema
```

  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Native SDK">

```ts
import { schema, table, t } from "spacetimedb/server"

const spacetime = schema({
  user: table(
    { public: true },
    { id: t.string().primaryKey(), name: t.string() },
  ),
})

// The exported binding's name is the reducer name.
export const user_upsert = spacetime.reducer(
  { id: t.string(), name: t.string() },
  (ctx, { id, name }) => {
    ctx.db.user.insert({ id, name })
  },
)

export default spacetime
```

  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

The authoring flow is:

1. Declare value types, tables, and endpoint groups.
2. Assemble a module with `StdbModule.make(...).addTables(...).add(...)`.
3. Implement each group with `StdbBuilder.group(...)`.
4. Build the native module export with `build(...)` from
   `effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`.

## Dev Loop

Build modules with the native SpaceTimeDB CLI. Put the build and client
generation commands behind package scripts:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "spacetime build --module-path .",
    "generate-client": "spacetime generate --lang typescript --js-path ./dist/bundle.js --out-dir ./src/generated --yes"
  }
}
```

Then run the scripts from the module package:

```sh
bun run build
bun run generate-client
```

:::tip

Use `build` before publishing a module and `generate-client` after changing the
module contract.

:::

:::note

Plain `spacetime generate` is the default and its `DbConnection` can be passed
directly to the Effect client. Projects that do not want generated TypeScript in
their stricter type graph can use the published quarantined artifact pipeline
and a spec-typed facade described in [Codegen](/core-concepts/clients/codegen).

:::

## Testing your module off-host

A module entry statically imports the host-only compiler (`build` from
`effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`). To import that entry in Vitest without a
real SpaceTimeDB host, alias the host syscalls to the shipped stub and inline the
`spacetimedb` package:

```ts
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config"
import { spacetimeSysAlias } from "effect-spacetimedb/testing"

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    server: { deps: { inline: ["spacetimedb"] } },
  },
  resolve: {
    alias: { ...spacetimeSysAlias },
  },
})
```

The stub keeps `console` and the deterministic backstops usable off-host, so
importing or building a module entry in tests does not require a running host.

## Next Pages

- [Reducers](/core-concepts/functions/reducers)
- [Tables / Column Types](/core-concepts/tables/column-types)
- [Runtime model](/the-effect-layer/runtime-model)
- [SpacetimeDB coverage map](/spacetimedb-coverage)
- [Reference](/reference)

# Source: /reference

---
draft: false
title: Reference
description: Entrypoints, capability scopes, value-type helpers, and declared-error rules.
sidebar:
  order: 99
---

This is a curated reference for the public surface. It is intentionally
hand-written; there is no generated API reference.

## Entrypoints

| Entrypoint | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `effect-spacetimedb` | Contract builders, value types, tables, declared errors, module assembly, builder APIs, and client projection. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/client` | WebSocket generated-client adapters and client transport helpers. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/client/atom` | Effect Atom bindings for React consumers; needs the optional `@effect/atom-react` and `react` peers. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/codegen` | Quarantined client generation: runs the native generator and emits an erased artifact. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/server` | Advanced server primitives for integrations that bypass normal builder flow. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler` | Host-only compiler entrypoint for module entries; import `build` from here. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/server-polyfills` | Standalone side-effect import for host compatibility shims; normal module entries get these through `server-compiler`. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/dev-server` | Programmatic local `spacetimedb-standalone` orchestration for tests and tools that publish a prebuilt bundle. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/testing` | Test-oriented helpers, package-local fixtures, and the `spacetimeSysAlias` preset for off-host server imports. |
| `effect-spacetimedb/testing/spacetime-sys` | Direct `spacetime:sys` host-surface stub for off-host module imports. |

Normal module authors usually need only `effect-spacetimedb` and, for WebSocket
sessions, `effect-spacetimedb/client`.

## Capability Scoping

| Scope | Allowed accessors |
| --- | --- |
| reducer, lifecycle | `Db`, `ReducerCtx`, `MutationCtx` |
| procedure outside a transaction | platform `Http`, `Tx`, `ProcedureCtx` |
| `Tx.run(...)` or `HttpTx.run(...)` body | `Db`, `MutationCtx`, transaction context |
| HTTP handler | `HttpTx`, `HttpHandlerCtx` |
| sender view | `ReadonlyDb`, `From`, `ViewCtx` |
| anonymous view | `ReadonlyDb`, `From`, `AnonymousViewCtx` |

Use `MutationCtx` for helpers that must run in both reducers and transaction
bodies. Do not yield accessors from another module.

## Value-Type Cheat Sheet

| Helper | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Stdb.string(schema?)` | SATS string with optional Effect schema branding or checks. |
| `Stdb.u8` / `u16` / `u32` / `u64` | Unsigned integer widths with constructor-owned bounds. |
| `Stdb.u128` / `u256` | Wide unsigned integer widths backed by `bigint`. |
| `Stdb.i8` / `i16` / `i32` / `i64` | Signed integer widths. |
| `Stdb.i128` / `i256` | Wide signed integer widths backed by `bigint`. |
| `Stdb.f32()` / `f64()` | Floating-point value types. |
| `Stdb.bigint()` | `bigint` authored value lowered to a SATS string for JSON-safe large numbers. |
| `Stdb.bool()` | Boolean value. |
| `Stdb.bytes()` | `Uint8Array` byte array. |
| `Stdb.identity()` / `connectionId()` | Native SpacetimeDB identity and connection id values. |
| `Stdb.timestamp()` / `timeDuration()` / `uuid()` | Native timestamp, duration, and UUID values. |
| `Stdb.scheduleAt()` | Scheduled-table `scheduledAt` column value type. |
| `Stdb.option(T)` | Nullable value type, decoded as `T` or `undefined`. |
| `Stdb.optional(T)` | Optional struct field annotation. |
| `T.optional()` | Optional table column annotation. |
| `Stdb.array(T)` | SATS array/list. |
| `Stdb.struct({...})` | Named object shape for params, rows, returns, and errors. |
| `Stdb.sum({...})` | Tagged union with payload variants; key- and index-capable, never auto-increment. |
| `T.named("Name")` | Set the generated SATS/client type name for an anonymous struct, sum, or string-literal enum; the default name is content-addressed. |
| `Stdb.enum("A", "B")` / `enumType(...)` | Unit-variant SATS enum; prefer namespace form because `enum` cannot be named-imported. |
| `Stdb.unit()` | Unit value for empty scheduled procedure returns, result branches, and sum payloads. |
| `Stdb.literal(...)` | String, number, or boolean literal values; string literals lower to enums. |
| `Stdb.result(Ok, Err)` | Result envelope value type. |
| `Stdb.dbCodec(T)` / `httpCodec(T)` / `wsCodec(T)` | Transport codecs for DB/host, HTTP JSON, and generated WebSocket client shapes. |
| `Stdb.lazy(() => T)` | Recursive value type reference. |
| `Stdb.custom(schema, { type })` | Custom schema with explicit SpaceTimeDB type lowering. |

See [Value Types](/the-effect-layer/value-types) for the canonical catalog with
TypeScript values, SATS lowering, bounds, and transport encoding notes.

## Authoring API

| Surface | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `Stdb.table(...)` / `scheduledTable(...)` | Declare persistent, event, and scheduled tables. |
| `Stdb.index(...)` / `unique(...)` | Declare table indexes and uniqueness constraints. |
| `Stdb.StdbFn.reducer(...)` / `procedure(...)` / `scheduledReducer(...)` / `scheduledProcedure(...)` / `view(...)` / `anonymousView(...)` | Declare callable and view endpoints. |
| `Stdb.StdbGroup.make(...)` / `Stdb.StdbHttpGroup.make(...)` | Group reducers/procedures/views and HTTP routes. |
| `Stdb.StdbHttp.*` | Declare typed and raw HTTP handlers. |
| `Stdb.StdbModule.make(...)` | Assemble tables, callable groups, HTTP groups, lifecycle, and settings. |
| `Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(...)` / `groupChecked(...)` / `groupPrechecked(...)` / `lifecycle(...)` | Attach Effect implementations to an assembled module. |
| `Stdb.project(Module)` | Build client projections, targets, and generated-client adapters. |
| `Stdb.toHttpApi(Module)` / `httpApiBaseUrl(...)` | Project typed HTTP routes into Effect `HttpApi`. |
| `Stdb.ScheduleAt.*` | Build scheduled table `scheduledAt` values. |
| `Stdb.validate(...)` / `assertValid(...)` / `formatModuleDiagnostics(...)` | Run module validation manually. |

Builder impl values are sealed. `GroupImpl<Name, RuntimeR, ModuleName>` and
`LifecycleImpl<Hooks, RuntimeR, ModuleName>` expose only build-time group,
lifecycle, runtime-requirement, and module-identity phantoms; handler
definitions are private to the builder pipeline. The module-name parameter
defaults to `string` so older two-argument annotations still compile, but
`build(...)` and `plan(...)` reject widened impl annotations. Keep
implementation arrays inferred with `as const` when storing them before
`build(...)`.

`groupPrechecked(...)` returns `GroupImpl<Name, never>` for handler records that
already satisfy `GroupCheckedHandlers<Module, Name>`. That annotation allows only
the server-context services valid for each endpoint kind and the current module's
accessors. Cross-module accessors are rejected through the Effect requirements
channel; the legacy `effect-spacetimedb/server` section/single-handler
validators remain module-blind for compatibility, while transaction helpers keep
branded residual runner requirements for transaction-family coherence. Use
`group(...)` when a handler intentionally requires a custom service and provide a
runtime to `build(...)`.

## Declared Error Catalog

Declared errors are created with a namespace:

```ts
const AppErrors = Stdb.errors.namespace("App")({
  UserMissing: Stdb.error({ userId: Stdb.string(UserId) }, { status: 404 }),
})
```

The catalog value supplies:

| Surface | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| generated classes | Fail directly from handlers with typed payloads. |
| `.schema` | Decode and encode the declared error envelope. |
| `.tags` | Known wire tags for client and route projection. |
| `.pick(...)` | Narrow a catalog to selected declared errors. |

:::caution

Only Effect failures are encoded as declared errors. Defects remain defects.

:::

## Runtime And Client Error Types

| Type | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `ReducerAsyncNotAllowedError` | Async, promises, timers, microtasks, or `Effect.sleep` in synchronous server handlers. |
| `ReducerGlobalRandomNotAllowedError` | Global `Math.random` use in guarded server runtime. |
| `ReducerWallClockNotAllowedError` | Ambient `Date.now()` or no-argument `new Date()` in guarded server runtime. |
| `StdbHostCallError` | Generic host ABI call failure. |
| `StdbUniqueAlreadyExistsError` / `StdbNoSuchRowError` / `StdbAutoIncOverflowError` / `StdbScheduleDelayTooLongError` | Typed native host failures. |
| `StdbDecodeError` | Contract decode failure. |
| `CallFailure<E>` / `RawCallFailure<E>` | Projected client call failure unions. |
| `RemoteRejectedError` / `TransportError` / `DomainCallError<E>` | Projected client remote, transport, and raw declared-error failures. |
| `WsConnectError` / `WsConnectTimeoutError` | WebSocket acquisition failed, or did not complete in time. |
| `ConnectionLostError` | An established session was invalidated; the call's outcome is unknown. |
| `GeneratedArtifactShapeError` | The generated client is missing relations the contract declares. |

| Clients / Unreal | [SpacetimeDB -> Unreal](https://spacetimedb.com/docs/clients/unreal) | not-supported | effect-spacetimedb targets TypeScript/Effect. |
| Effect Layer / Value-Type Design | N/A | native | [Value-Type Design](/the-effect-layer/value-type-design) |
| Effect Layer / Value Representations | N/A | native | [Value Representations](/the-effect-layer/value-representations) |
| Effect Layer / Value Types | N/A | native | [Value Types](/the-effect-layer/value-types) |
| Effect Layer / Option vs Optional | N/A | native | [Option vs Optional](/the-effect-layer/option-vs-optional) |
| Effect Layer / Runtime Model | N/A | native | [Runtime Model](/the-effect-layer/runtime-model) |
| Effect Layer / Randomness & Determinism | N/A | native | [Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism) |
| Effect Layer / Migrating From Native SDK | N/A | native | [Migrating From Native SDK](/the-effect-layer/migrating-from-native-sdk) |

# Source: /the-effect-layer/migrating-from-native-sdk

---
draft: false
title: Migrating From Native SDK Shape
description: Move from native SpaceTimeDB module code to effect-spacetimedb contracts incrementally.
sidebar:
  order: 8
---

import { TabItem, Tabs } from "@astrojs/starlight/components";

:::tip

You do not need to rewrite a whole module at once. Start by modeling the module
contract, then move handlers behind the typed builder group by group.

:::

## The Same Module, Both Ways

The native module and the equivalent effect-spacetimedb contract — declare the
shape, then implement handlers behind the typed group:

<Tabs syncKey="impl">
  <TabItem label="Native SDK">

```ts
import { schema, table, t } from "spacetimedb/server"

const spacetime = schema({
  user: table(
    { public: true },
    { id: t.string().primaryKey(), name: t.string() },
  ),
})

export const user_upsert = spacetime.reducer(
  { id: t.string(), name: t.string() },
  (ctx, { id, name }) => {
    ctx.db.user.insert({ id, name })
  },
)

export default spacetime
```

  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="effect-spacetimedb">

```ts
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

// 1. declare the contract
const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  public: true,
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string().primaryKey(),
    name: Stdb.string(),
  },
})

const Users = Stdb.StdbGroup.make("Users").add(
  Stdb.StdbFn.reducer("user_upsert", {
    params: Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string(), name: Stdb.string() }),
  }),
)

const Module = Stdb.StdbModule.make("app").addTables(user).add(Users)
const { Db } = Module

// 2. implement handlers behind the typed group
const UsersLive = Stdb.StdbBuilder.group(Module, "Users", {
  user_upsert: (args) =>
    Effect.gen(function* () {
      const db = yield* Db
      yield* db.user.insert(args)
    }),
})
```

  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

## Native Shape To Contract Shape

| Native concept | effect-spacetimedb concept |
| --- | --- |
| reducer function export | `StdbFn.reducer(...)` in a callable group |
| procedure function export | `StdbFn.procedure(...)` in a callable group |
| table builder | `Stdb.table(...)` bound to a variable |
| `reducer`/`procedure` `onSchedule` option | `StdbFn.scheduledReducer(...)` or `scheduledProcedure(...)` |
| HTTP handler export | `StdbHttpGroup` plus `StdbBuilder.group(...)` |

Schedules are registered on the function, not the table: `StdbFn.scheduledReducer(...)`
and `scheduledProcedure(...)` compile to the native `onSchedule` option, which is
where SpacetimeDB now expects the binding. If you are porting a module that
passes `scheduled` to `table(...)`, that registration is deprecated upstream —
drop it and declare the scheduled callable instead.

## Suggested Order

1. Move schemas and table declarations into leaf files.
2. Declare groups without changing runtime behavior.
3. Assemble a module and destructure the typed accessors.
4. Port handlers one group at a time.
5. Generate the client and replace ad hoc call sites with projected clients.

Keep the runtime constraints in mind: module handlers must remain synchronous,
deterministic, and transactional. Network calls, timers, and secrets belong
outside reducers and are passed in as arguments or handled by external services.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/option-vs-optional

---
draft: false
title: Stdb.option vs Stdb.optional
description: Choose value nullability or field optionality intentionally.
sidebar:
  order: 6
---

`Stdb.option(T)` is a nullable value type. Its decoded TypeScript value is
`T | undefined`, and its SATS wire type is `option<T>`. Use it anywhere a value
type is allowed: arguments, array elements, table columns, nested types, and
struct fields. In a struct field, the key is still required.

`Stdb.optional(T)` and `.optional()` are field or column optionality annotations.
They mean the struct field or table column itself may be omitted. In struct and
callable param fields they lower to the same SATS `option<T>` wire type as
`Stdb.option(T)`.

Rule of thumb:

- Use `Stdb.option` for standalone nullable values and fields that are always
  present but may be none.
- Use `Stdb.optional` or `.optional()` when the property or column may be
  omitted.

The wire shape is the same for struct fields; the TypeScript shape differs:
`Stdb.optional(T)` gives `x?: T`, while `Stdb.option(T)` gives
`x: T | undefined`.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism

---
draft: false
title: Randomness And Determinism
description: Deterministic randomness for reducers, and why it is not secret.
sidebar:
  order: 5
---

Reducers must be deterministic. Every replica needs to reproduce the same result
from the same logged inputs, so module code should use host-provided time and
randomness rather than ambient JavaScript globals.

## Reducer Randomness

Inside Effect-based reducers, use `Random.*` from `effect/Random`. The constrained server
runtime wires Effect randomness to the call context's deterministic random
stream.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Random from "effect/Random"

const roll = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const die = yield* Random.nextIntBetween(1, 6)
  const fraction = yield* Random.next
  return { die, fraction }
})
```

:::caution

Do not call global `Math.random` in reducers, procedures, views, or HTTP handler
effects. Development guards replace it with a throwing stub so accidental use
fails early.

:::

## Wall Clock

Use the call timestamp supplied by the current context instead of ambient clock
globals. In guarded development runs, `Date.now()` and no-argument `new Date()`
throw `ReducerWallClockNotAllowedError`; `Math.random` throws
`ReducerGlobalRandomNotAllowedError`; suspended Effects, promises, timers, and
microtasks throw `ReducerAsyncNotAllowedError`.

The Effect clock is wired to the same transaction timestamp, so `Effect.Clock`
and `DateTime.now` are deterministic inside server handlers.

## UUID Helpers

Reducer, transaction, and HTTP handler contexts expose deterministic UUID
helpers. Use `ctx.newUuidV4()` and `ctx.newUuidV7()` when a row needs a stable
identifier produced inside server module code.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Effect from "effect/Effect"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

declare const Module: Stdb.AnyStdbModule

const { ReducerCtx } = Module

const ids = Effect.gen(function* () {
  const ctx = yield* ReducerCtx
  return {
    randomId: ctx.newUuidV4(),
    timeSortableId: ctx.newUuidV7(),
  }
})
```

## Runtime Wiring

The constrained server runtime wires `Random.*` from `effect/Random` to the
current SpaceTimeDB call context through `ctx.random`, so helpers such as
`Random.next`, `Random.nextIntBetween`, and `Random.shuffle` consume the same
deterministic stream exposed by the host.

SpaceTimeDB replaces `Math.random` in module runtimes. In guarded development
runs, `effect-spacetimedb` also replaces it with a throwing guard so accidental
callers fail loudly in tests and CI. The runtime still installs a deterministic
fallback as a non-semantic backstop for stray library paths, but application
logic should not depend on it.

The host random stream is deterministic and replica-reproducible. Supplying a
developer-chosen seed makes results more reproducible, not more secret.

## Strength

Reducer randomness is useful for gameplay-grade choices: shuffles, loot rolls,
procedural content, and reproducible simulations. It is not appropriate for
secrets, tokens, authentication, anti-cheat, or any security-sensitive value.

If a value must be unpredictable, generate it outside the deterministic reducer
with a trusted source of entropy and pass it in as an argument.

## Rules

- Use `Random.*` from `effect/Random` inside server handlers.
- Use context randomness only at low-level interop boundaries.
- Never use `Math.random` for server semantics.
- Never use ambient wall-clock reads for committed server semantics.
- Treat reducer randomness as deterministic and non-cryptographic.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/runtime-model

---
draft: false
title: Runtime Model
description: How Effect programs run inside SpaceTimeDB's synchronous, deterministic module host.
sidebar:
  order: 1
---

SpaceTimeDB runs module code inside a strict host contract: each reducer,
procedure, view, HTTP handler, and lifecycle handler is synchronous,
run-to-completion, single-transaction where applicable, and deterministic.
`effect-spacetimedb` runs Effect programs inside that contract rather than
pretending the module runtime is a normal JavaScript environment.

## Synchronous Effects Only

:::caution

Handler effects must complete in one synchronous pass. Do not use promises,
`async` functions, timers, `queueMicrotask`, or `Effect.sleep` in server module
handlers. Development guards make these operations fail loudly so code that
would suspend the module host is caught early.

:::

Finalizers from scoped Effects still run synchronously before the host commits or
rolls back, so `Effect.acquireRelease` is safe when the acquired resource is
bounded to the current call.

At the host boundary, each reducer, procedure, view, HTTP handler, and lifecycle
handler is executed with the sync runner and `Scheduler.PreventSchedulerYield`.
Anything that suspends the fiber surfaces as `ReducerAsyncNotAllowedError`.
`Effect.sleep` fails with the same error in all modes. Guarded development runs
also replace timer and microtask globals with throwing stubs so accidental use
fails before a module is published.

## Determinism

Every replica must replay the same input log to the same state. Use
`Random.*` from `effect/Random` for deterministic randomness and use the call
timestamp for time. Do not call `Math.random`, `Date.now`, or
`performance.now` for server semantics. See
[Randomness & Determinism](/the-effect-layer/randomness-and-determinism) for
the full guard and UUID-helper contract.

Determinism is reproducibility, not secrecy. Generate tokens, secrets, and
cryptographically unpredictable values outside the reducer and pass them in.

The server runtime wires `Random.*` from `effect/Random` to `ctx.random`. It also
provides the Effect clock from `ctx.timestamp`, so `Effect.Clock` and
`DateTime.now` reflect the transaction timestamp. In guarded development runs,
`Math.random`, `Date.now()`, and no-argument `new Date()` throw deterministic
runtime errors; explicit conversions such as `new Date(123)`, `Date.parse`, and
`Date.UTC` remain available.

## Transactions

Reducers run inside one ambient writable transaction and may yield `Db`
directly. Procedures and HTTP handlers open transactions explicitly with `Tx` or
`HttpTx`. Transaction bodies may be retried after optimistic commit conflicts,
so keep them pure database work and put external side effects outside them.

Only mutable transactions exist in the JavaScript host. SpaceTimeDB exposes no
read-only transaction for procedures; a read-only transaction would be a
type-level convention, not a host feature. A procedure that opens several
transactions has no automatic rollback across them, so multi-step workflows need
their own status rows and cleanup process.

## Host Call Failures

Host ABI calls can fail before user code gets a normal return value. Generic or
unrecognized host failures surface as `StdbHostCallError` with the operation
label and original cause. Four native SpaceTimeDB host errors are split out so
handlers can branch without string-sniffing causes:

- `StdbUniqueAlreadyExistsError`
- `StdbAutoIncOverflowError`
- `StdbNoSuchRowError`
- `StdbScheduleDelayTooLongError`

Each carries `{ op, cause }`, matching `StdbHostCallError`. Branch on a specific
tag only when a handler has a real recovery path, such as translating a unique
constraint collision into a declared domain error. Otherwise let the error
propagate so the host-boundary throw keeps the operation label and original
cause.

The classifier uses native error class names rather than `instanceof`, because
ordinary server runtime files cannot value-import `spacetimedb/server` without
loading the host-only syscall surface. Dependency bumps should re-check the
native server error-name surface.

## Observability

Tracing is disabled on the server. Effect spans are not exported from a reducer,
and the default tracer would allocate span ids from ambient randomness, so
server effects run with tracing off. `Effect.fn` still works; it produces a noop
span.

`Effect.log*` bridges to the host console through the runtime logger. Logs
emitted while a reducer, procedure, HTTP handler, view, or lifecycle handler runs
carry the module, handler, and kind. Caller-scoped handlers also annotate the
sender identity; anonymous views and HTTP handlers omit sender.

## Polyfills And Guarded Mode

SpaceTimeDB's module runtime is a minimal JavaScript environment. The server
compat layer installs small shims only when they are missing:

- a deterministic `Math.random` fallback, used only as a library backstop,
- immediate-execution timer shims and no-op clear functions.

Module entrypoints import `effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler`, which installs
the server compatibility polyfills before exposing `build`. Native
`spacetime build` preserves that side-effectful compiler entrypoint.

The constrained runtime has a production mode and a guarded development mode.
Guarded mode is selected automatically under tests and temporarily swaps
forbidden globals for throwing stubs for the duration of each call, restoring
them afterward. Code that passes guarded mode behaves deterministically in the
host.

## Quick Rules

- Keep handler bodies synchronous.
- Use `Random.*` from `effect/Random`, not `Math.random`.
- Use call timestamps, not ambient clocks.
- Write directly in reducers; use `tx.run(...)` in procedures and HTTP handlers.
- Keep transaction bodies idempotent and database-only.
- Import `effect-spacetimedb/server-compiler` in module entrypoints; it installs
  the server polyfills without a separate bundle prelude injection.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/value-representations

---
draft: false
title: Value Representations
description: Authored values, schema-encoded values, and host JavaScript values.
sidebar:
  order: 4
---

`effect-spacetimedb` works with three related value shapes:

- **Authored Type values** are what handlers and typed clients use.
- **Schema encoded values** are the wire side of Effect schema codecs, especially
  for typed HTTP request and response bodies.
- **Host JS values** are the shapes accepted by SpaceTimeDB's JavaScript host for
  reducer arguments, table rows, lookup keys, and handler returns.

The host representation is close to authored values but not identical to schema
encoded values. The library normalizes host values before schema decoding so
handlers can work with authored Type values.

See [Value Types](/the-effect-layer/value-types) for the canonical helper
catalog. This page focuses on transport and encoding semantics.

## Compatibility Rules

- Absent optional struct fields and absent `Stdb.option` fields are omitted from
  host structs.
- Result host input accepts `{ ok }` and `{ err }` envelopes, then normalizes
  them to schema tagged result shapes.
- Sum host input uses authored tagged values: `{ tag }` for unit variants and
  `{ tag, value }` for payload variants.
- Primitive, literal, custom, and no-descriptor leaves delegate to their schema
  encoder.

HTTP JSON has its own representation profile. It rewrites exact option
envelopes, canonicalizes declared field names for SATS JSON, and normalizes
responses back to declared field names where needed.

## Result Envelopes

Result values are the main host/schema asymmetry. Host values use `{ ok }` /
`{ err }` envelopes, while the Effect schema codec expects tagged
`{ tag, value }` result envelopes. DB and WebSocket host decoders normalize the
host envelope before schema decoding, and handler return encoding emits the
native `{ ok }` / `{ err }` shape.

## Literal And Sum Tags

Sum host values use authored tagged shapes: `{ tag }` for unit variants and
`{ tag, value }` for variants with payloads.

String `Stdb.literal(...)` values also use authored tags on DB/host and HTTP
paths when the authored value is a valid SpaceTimeDB identifier. Values that are
not valid identifiers use a generated-client-safe PascalCase SATS tag while
decoding back to the authored value. Generated-client WebSocket calls accept the
PascalCase convention; DB and HTTP profiles keep authored tags where SATS
permits them.

## Numeric And Binary Profiles

- `u8`/`u16`/`u32` and `i8`/`i16`/`i32` are authored as `number` and checked at
  their constructor-owned integer bounds.
- `u64`/`u128`/`u256` and `i64`/`i128`/`i256` are authored as `bigint`, checked
  at their fixed-width bounds, and remain `bigint` in DB and WebSocket shapes.
- `Stdb.bigint()` is authored as `bigint` but lowers to a SATS string so large
  arbitrary integers can move through JSON safely.
- `Stdb.f32()` and `Stdb.f64()` use `number`. DB and generated WebSocket shapes
  preserve native `NaN`/`Infinity`; HTTP JSON rejects non-finite values because
  JSON has no representation for them.
- `Stdb.bytes()` is a `Uint8Array` byte array.

## Native Host Values

`Stdb.timestamp()`, `Stdb.timeDuration()`, `Stdb.uuid()`,
`Stdb.identity()`, and `Stdb.connectionId()` use the native SpacetimeDB classes
in authored server and generated-client values. Their HTTP JSON shape is the
schema-encoded representation produced by `Stdb.httpCodec(...)`.

These classes validate their own input, and construction is where a malformed
value is caught: a non-integer number, a boolean, an array, `null`, a blank
string, or a string that is not valid hex or a valid UUID is refused outright.
Decoding runs that check inside the library's typed boundary, so an HTTP body
carrying `{"__identity__": "not-hex"}` or `{"__uuid__": [42]}` fails with
`StdbDecodeError` in the error channel instead of surfacing as a raw
`TypeError` defect.

## HTTP JSON Profile

HTTP JSON input preparation rewrites exact `{ some: value }` option envelopes,
drops unknown struct fields, canonicalizes declared field names to snake case,
and prepares literal and sum payloads for SATS JSON.

Output normalization accepts SpacetimeDB HTTP JSON shapes, falls back to
schema-AST normalization when a value is not in a descriptor-specific shape,
recurses into bare options, and rebinds canonical snake-case struct fields back
to declared field names.

String literal SATS enum objects use the schema variant as the JSON object key
or `{ tag }` value. HTTP JSON payloads emitted by this package use schema tags;
raw SATS JSON callers should emit those same tags and deploy in the same rollout
as any module republish that changes persisted enum schemas.

## Value Codecs

Use `Stdb.dbCodec(T)` for host/DB values, `Stdb.httpCodec(T)` for HTTP JSON,
and `Stdb.wsCodec(T)` for generated WebSocket client values. The WebSocket codec
accepts the generated client's PascalCase enum tags for sums and string
literals, while DB and HTTP profiles keep authored tags where SATS permits them.

## Single Traversal Rule

Per-kind traversal logic lives in the value-type descriptor fold. Representation
profiles are layered over that traversal so host, HTTP, and WebSocket codecs do
not drift into independent descriptor dispatch rules.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/value-type-design

---
draft: false
title: Value-Type Design
description: Why Stdb value types are opaque wrappers around Effect schemas.
sidebar:
  order: 2
---

An `Stdb.*` value type wraps an Effect schema rather than being a plain schema.
That design is deliberate: SpaceTimeDB declaration sites must reject raw Effect
schemas at compile time, while application code still needs ordinary schemas for
decode, encode, HTTP bodies, and domain logic.

## The Two Jobs

A value type must:

1. Reuse an Effect schema for TypeScript values and JSON codecs.
2. Carry SpaceTimeDB SATS information so tables, params, returns, and errors
   lower to native types.

Effect annotations preserve runtime metadata, but TypeScript cannot see whether
a schema has a particular annotation. Phantom type markers on schemas are also
fragile because Effect transforms rebuild schema types and strip the marker.

## Why Annotations Are Not Enough

Two Effect behaviors constrain the design:

- **Annotations are runtime-only at the type level.** `effect-spacetimedb`
  stores the real SATS information as schema annotations, and those annotations
  survive transforms. But a schema with an annotation and a schema without one
  have the same TypeScript type, so annotations alone cannot make raw schemas in
  SATS positions a compile-time error.
- **Schema transforms rebuild schema types.** `.pipe`, `.check`, `.brand`, and
  `.annotate` return the canonical schema type and drop any phantom property
  added by a cast. That is sound: the transform creates a new schema object that
  does not carry the cast-on property at runtime.

## The Trilemma

Enforcing SATS positions at compile time, keeping value types as plain Effect
schemas, and staying robust under composition are mutually exclusive:

| Approach | Compile-time rejection of raw schemas | Value type is a plain Effect schema | Robust under transforms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phantom marker on schema type | Yes | Yes | No; transforms strip the marker. |
| Opaque wrapper | Yes | No; use `.schema` to unwrap. | Yes |
| Annotations only | No; validate at module build time. | Yes | Yes |

`effect-spacetimedb` chooses the opaque wrapper. The wrapper is not itself a
schema; unwrap with `.schema` when ordinary Effect schema interop is required.

This keeps one important guarantee: raw schemas are rejected in SATS positions at
compile time. It also avoids "tag must be last" bugs where a refinement or brand
accidentally strips a marker.

## Accepted Tradeoffs

- **`.schema` unwraps a value type to its Effect schema** for decode/encode,
  `Schema.*` combinators, and HTTP request/response bodies.
- **All refinement happens inside the constructor.** Each scalar takes either no
  schema or one Effect schema. Branding is just `Schema.brand(...)` on the
  passed schema, not a privileged argument.
- **Numeric width belongs to the constructor.** `Stdb.u16()` always enforces the
  `[0, 65535]` range because Effect range checks do not narrow the TypeScript
  type enough for SATS width proof at the call site.

## Recommended Pattern

For branded domain values, keep the raw Effect schema as the source of truth and
wrap it inline at SpaceTimeDB boundaries:

```ts
const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId"))

Stdb.string(UserId) // table fields, params, returns, error fields
```

Avoid keeping parallel aliases such as a raw `UserId` schema and a separate
`UserIdT` value-type wrapper for the same domain id. Wrap the domain schema at
declaration sites. Generic, non-branded SATS scalars reused across many fields
may be kept as value-type aliases.

For generic SATS values reused across many fields, keep a value-type alias:

```ts
const ShortString = Stdb.string(Schema.String.pipe(Schema.minLength(1)))
```

Composites and rows are the value types you usually keep. A row's `.schema`
decodes the whole row.

## Literal Unions

If a union exists for SpaceTimeDB use, declare it with `Stdb.literal(...)`. It
lowers to a SATS enum on the wire and decodes to the literal TypeScript union.

String literal enum tags preserve authored strings verbatim on DB/host and HTTP
paths when the authored value is a valid SpaceTimeDB identifier. Non-identifier
values use a generated-client-safe PascalCase tag in the SATS schema while still
decoding to the authored value. Official generated clients expose schema
variants through SpaceTimeDB's PascalCase convention, so
`Stdb.literal("pending_review")` encodes as `{ tag: "pending_review" }` for DB
and HTTP and as `{ tag: "PendingReview" }` for generated-client WebSocket calls.

HTTP JSON tools should send the schema SATS tag. Existing modules with persisted
enum columns may need a reset or hand-written migration when republished because
changing SATS variant names changes the column type identity.

Numeric `Stdb.literal(...)` values lower to `f64`; non-finite numbers and unsafe
integers beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` are rejected.

If the union is a core shared domain schema also consumed by HTTP DTOs, keep
`Stdb.custom(CoreSchema, { type: <string scalar> })` so the values have one
source of truth. A lint rule enforces that custom inline literals do not replace
`Stdb.literal(...)` for local SATS-only unions.

## Optional Fields

`Stdb.optional(...)`, table-column `.optional()`, and `Stdb.option(...)` all
lower to SATS `option<T>` when a struct is materialized. They differ in the
TypeScript surface: field-level optionality gives `key?: T`, while
`Stdb.option(...)` gives a required `key: T | undefined` value. Prefer
`Stdb.option(...)` for fields constructed from computed possibly-undefined
values.

## Alternative Design

If compile-time rejection were not required, annotations-only value types would
be simpler and more Effect-native: the value type would be a plain schema, with
raw schemas in SATS positions caught by module validation instead of typecheck.
This package chooses the compile-time guarantee over that simpler interop model.


---

# Source: /the-effect-layer/value-types

---
draft: false
title: Value Types
description: Canonical value-type helper catalog for authored TypeScript values, SATS lowering, and transport codecs.
sidebar:
  order: 3
---

Value types wrap Effect schemas with the SpaceTimeDB type information needed for
tables, call params, returns, declared errors, HTTP routes, and generated
clients.

```typescript twoslash
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema"
import * as Stdb from "effect-spacetimedb"

const UserId = Schema.String.pipe(Schema.brand("UserId"))

const user = Stdb.table("user", {
  columns: {
    id: Stdb.string(UserId).primaryKey(),
    level: Stdb.u32(),
    credits: Stdb.bigint(),
    createdAt: Stdb.timestamp(),
  },
})
```

Use namespace form for helpers, including `Stdb.enum(...)`; `enum` cannot be a
named import in JavaScript.

## Scalar Helpers

| Helper | Authored TypeScript value | SATS lowering | Bounds / encoding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Stdb.string(schema?)` | `string` or branded string | `string` | Optional schema refines the authored value. |
| `Stdb.bool(schema?)` | `boolean` or branded boolean | `bool` | Optional schema refines the authored value. |
| `Stdb.u8()` / `u16()` / `u32()` | `number` | unsigned integer width | Constructor checks `0..2^8-1`, `0..2^16-1`, or `0..2^32-1`. |
| `Stdb.i8()` / `i16()` / `i32()` | `number` | signed integer width | Constructor checks `-(2^(n-1))..2^(n-1)-1`. |
| `Stdb.u64()` / `u128()` / `u256()` | `bigint` | unsigned integer width | Constructor checks `0..2^n-1`; DB and generated-client transports keep `bigint`. |
| `Stdb.i64()` / `i128()` / `i256()` | `bigint` | signed integer width | Constructor checks `-(2^(n-1))..2^(n-1)-1`; DB and generated-client transports keep `bigint`. |
| `Stdb.f32()` / `f64()` | `number` | `f32` / `f64` | DB and WebSocket profiles preserve `NaN`/`Infinity`; HTTP JSON rejects non-finite numbers. |
| `Stdb.bigint()` | `bigint` | `string` | JSON-safe arbitrary-size integer encoded through `Schema.BigIntFromString`. |
| `Stdb.bytes()` | `Uint8Array` | byte array | Host and generated-client values are byte arrays. |
| `Stdb.identity()` | `spacetimedb.Identity` | identity | Native identity object. |
| `Stdb.connectionId()` | `spacetimedb.ConnectionId` | connection id | Native connection id object. |
| `Stdb.timestamp()` | `spacetimedb.Timestamp` | timestamp | Native timestamp object, microseconds since Unix epoch. |
| `Stdb.timeDuration()` | `spacetimedb.TimeDuration` | time duration | Native duration object, microseconds. |
| `Stdb.scheduleAt()` | `spacetimedb.ScheduleAt` | schedule-at | Scheduled-table `scheduledAt` value type. |
| `Stdb.uuid()` | `spacetimedb.Uuid` | UUID | Native UUID object. |
| `Stdb.unit()` | `void` / `undefined` | unit | Empty payload marker for sums, results, and scheduled procedure returns. |

The five id-like natives — `Stdb.identity()`, `Stdb.connectionId()`,
`Stdb.timestamp()`, `Stdb.timeDuration()`, and `Stdb.uuid()` — validate at
construction: the SpacetimeDB constructors reject anything that is not a
`bigint`, an integer `number`, or a well-formed string, and a blank string is
not well-formed. Where such a value arrives from outside the process, that
rejection is reported as a typed `StdbDecodeError` on the decode boundary, not
as a defect, so a malformed `__identity__` or `__uuid__` in an HTTP body fails
the call rather than killing the fiber.

`Stdb.bigint()` is not the same as the fixed-width integer helpers. Use
`Stdb.bigint()` when the database column should be a SATS string carrying a
JSON-safe arbitrary integer. Use `i64`/`u64`/`i128`/`u128`/`i256`/`u256` when the
database column should be a native integer width and the authored value should
stay a `bigint`.

## Composite Helpers

| Helper | Authored TypeScript value | SATS lowering | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Stdb.array(T)` | `ReadonlyArray<TypeOf<T>>` | array/list | Recurses through the inner value type. |
| `Stdb.option(T)` | `TypeOf<T>` or `undefined` | `option<T>` | Present field whose value can be absent. |
| `Stdb.optional(T)` | optional struct field | `option<T>` in structs | Produces an optional TypeScript property. |
| `T.optional()` | optional table column | `option<T>` column | Column may be omitted on inserts. |
| `Stdb.struct({ ... })` | object | SATS struct | Use for rows, params, returns, and declared-error payloads. Anonymous structs get a content-addressed name unless you set one with [`.named(...)`](#type-names). |
| `Stdb.sum({ Tag: Payload })` | `{ tag, value? }` | SATS enum/sum | Unit payloads omit `value`; payload variants require `value`. Anonymous sums get a content-addressed name unless you set one with [`.named(...)`](#type-names). |
| `Stdb.enum("A", "B")` / `enumType(...)` | tagged unit variants | SATS enum | Unit-variant sums; prefer namespace form because `enum` cannot be named-imported. |
| `Stdb.literal(...)` | string, number, or boolean literal | string literals -> enum; numbers -> `f64`; booleans -> `bool` | String literal generated-client tags use SpaceTimeDB PascalCase. Numeric literals reject non-finite values and unsafe integers. |
| `Stdb.result(Ok, Err)` | Effect-style result envelope | SATS result | Normalizes host `{ ok }` / `{ err }` envelopes. |
| `Stdb.lazy(() => T)` | recursive value | lazy SATS type | Use for recursive structs or sums. |
| `Stdb.custom(schema, { type })` | schema-authored value | lowering of `type` | Keep the SpaceTimeDB lowering explicit when wrapping custom schemas. |

`Stdb.sum(...)` and `Stdb.enum(...)` columns are key- and index-capable. They
key on the whole encoded value, so each payload of a variant is its own key.
`.autoInc()` is not available on them. See
[Constraints](/core-concepts/tables/constraints) and
[Indexes](/core-concepts/tables/indexes).

## Type names

Anonymous `Stdb.struct(...)`, `Stdb.sum(...)`, and string-literal
`Stdb.literal(...)` types have no author-given name, so their generated
SATS/client type name is **content-addressed**: a stable hash of the shape such
as `EffectSpacetimeDbStruct...`. The hash is deterministic and collision-free,
but not readable.

Set a semantic name with `.named(...)`:

```ts
Stdb.struct({ id: Stdb.string() }).named("UserView") // generated type: `UserView`
```

The identifier is emitted verbatim, so prefer PascalCase (`MembershipView`) —
casing is not applied for you. JavaScript keywords, generated-client helper
names (`__*`), and callable-local bindings (`params`, `returnType`) are reserved.
When an anonymous value type is exported as a top-level reusable contract type,
keep the `.named(...)` identifier equal to the exported `const` identifier, for
example `export const UserView = Stdb.struct(...).named("UserView")`. Nested
inline names can use their own semantic payload names.

`table.row` is already named: it carries the table's PascalCase type name
automatically and reuses the table's single generated type, so a `user` table's
`user.row` lowers to the `User` type with no `.named(...)` needed. Return or nest
it directly:

```ts
Stdb.option(user.row) // reuses the table's `User` type, not a duplicate
```

`.named(...)` is distinct from `.name(...)`: `.name(...)` sets SpacetimeDB's
native builder column metadata and does not rename the generated type.

## Codecs

| Helper | Profile | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Stdb.dbCodec(T)` | SpaceTimeDB host / DB shape | Low-level host interop, table rows, reducer args, and generated server values. |
| `Stdb.httpCodec(T)` | HTTP JSON shape | Typed HTTP request and response bodies. Rejects non-finite floating-point numbers because JSON cannot carry them. |
| `Stdb.wsCodec(T)` | Generated WebSocket client shape | Client cache rows, subscription events, and callable payloads. Sum and string-literal tags are rewritten to the generated client's PascalCase convention. |

The public docs use this page as the helper catalog. See
[Value Representations](/the-effect-layer/value-representations) for the
transport profiles and [Column Types](/core-concepts/tables/column-types) for
table-specific usage.
